chapters.title: Plants and Animals Live Together
chapters.summary: In this chapter: animals living with plants; life in the soil; how animals use plants; listening to birds.

lessons.title: Animals Living with Plants

activities.prompt: Which animals might you spot living among plants?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Animals and Plants
activities.body: Animals are found wherever there are plants. They live on plants, around plants, and even underneath them. Elephants feed on grass. A moth can rest on a leaf. A caterpillar can chew a leaf. Earthworms can live on leaves and in soil. A woodpecker can sit on a tree trunk. Ants build nests using leaves. A frog, butterfly, and colourful stink bug can rest on leaves.
keyPoints: Animals live on, around and underneath plants.
Some animals feed on plants.
Others rest on leaves, trunks or soil.
activities.explanation: Plants give animals many places to live, rest and feed.

activities.prompt: How can the same leaf help both a moth and a caterpillar?
steps: A moth can rest on a leaf, so it has a place.
A caterpillar can chew a leaf, so it has food.
Both animals use the same plant in different ways.
Therefore, one leaf can help both animals.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Elephants feed on ______.
activities.hint: Look for the green plant that elephants eat.
activities.explanation: Elephants feed on grass.

activities.prompt: A moth can rest on a leaf.
activities.explanation: Yes, a moth can rest on a leaf.

activities.prompt: What can a caterpillar chew?
options: A leaf
A tree trunk
Some soil
A nest
activities.explanation: A caterpillar can chew a leaf.

activities.prompt: Match each animal with its place or action.
activities.explanation: These pairs show where animals rest or live, and what ants use.

activities.prompt: Which animal uses leaves to build its nest?
options: Ants
Frogs
Elephants
Earthworms
activities.explanation: Ants build their nest by using leaves.

activities.prompt: A caterpillar is placed on a leaf. What is most likely to happen?
options: It will chew the leaf.
It will feed on grass.
It will rest on a trunk.
It will sit on soil.

This mixes up a caterpillar with an elephant.
This uses a woodpecker's place, not a caterpillar's.
This uses an earthworm's place, not a caterpillar's.

activities.explanation: Caterpillars can chew leaves, so this is likely.

activities.prompt: Two animals share one leaf. One rests, and one chews it. Which animals are they?
options: A moth and a caterpillar.
A frog and a butterfly.
An elephant and a caterpillar.
A moth and a woodpecker.

A frog rests and a butterfly perches, but neither chews.
An elephant feeds on grass, while a caterpillar chews a leaf.
A moth can rest, but a woodpecker sits on a tree trunk.

activities.explanation: A moth can rest, and a caterpillar can chew, on a leaf.

activities.prompt: One leaf is being watched. Which group could be resting or perching on it?
options: A moth, a frog, and a butterfly.
An ant, a frog, and a caterpillar.
An elephant, a frog, and a woodpecker.
A woodpecker, a moth, and an ant.

The frog can rest, but the ant builds and the caterpillar chews.
The frog can rest, but the others use grass or a trunk.
The moth can rest, but the others sit or build with leaves.

activities.explanation: All three can rest or perch on a leaf.

activities.prompt: A child wants to check where earthworms can live. Which test is fair?
options: Place one on a leaf and one in soil.
Place one on a trunk and one in grass.
Place one on a leaf and one on a trunk.
Place one in soil and one beside a nest.

This uses places for a woodpecker and an elephant.
A leaf fits, but a trunk suits a woodpecker.
Soil fits, but a nest belongs to ants.

activities.explanation: Earthworms can live on leaves and in soil, so both fit.

activities.prompt: A child wants to observe an animal under a plant. Which test is best?
options: Watch an earthworm in soil below a plant.
Watch a moth on a leaf above soil.
Watch a frog on a leaf near a trunk.
Watch an elephant in grass near a tree.

A moth on a leaf is on the plant, not underneath.
A frog on a leaf is on the plant, not underneath.
Grass near a tree means around the plant, not underneath.

activities.explanation: The earthworm can live in soil below a plant.

lessons.title: Life in the Soil

activities.prompt: What tiny lives might be hiding beneath your feet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is soil like?
activities.body: Soil is the topmost layer of the Earth’s surface. Tiny pieces of broken rocks, old leaves, roots and stems help make it. Living and dead animals, including insects, are also part of soil. Many creatures live there. Some are too small to see. Earthworms and millipedes may appear after rain. Plants can grow, and seeds can wait in the soil for rain.
keyPoints: Soil has broken rocks, old plant parts, and animals.
Many creatures live in soil, but some are too small to see.
Rain helps earthworms, millipedes, plants, and seeds.
activities.explanation: Soil is busy with life, even when many of its tiny creatures cannot be seen.

activities.prompt: After rain, a child sees creatures and seeds in soil. Why?
steps: Earthworms and millipedes may appear because the soil is wet.
Some insects may emerge because they waited in soil for rains.
Seeds may sprout because rain or watering starts their growth.
Thus, soil is a home for many visible and tiny living things.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which tiny pieces help make soil?
options: Pieces of broken rocks
Old leaves
Grasshoppers
Ants
activities.explanation: Tiny pieces of broken rocks help make soil.

activities.prompt: Soil is the topmost layer of the Earth’s surface.
activities.explanation: Yes! Soil forms the topmost layer of the Earth’s surface.

activities.prompt: After rain, ______ and millipedes may appear in wet soil.
activities.hint: Think of the long, soft creature in soil.
activities.explanation: Earthworms and millipedes may appear when the soil is wet after rain.

activities.prompt: Which creatures may appear when soil is wet after rain?
options: Earthworms and millipedes
Ants and termites
Beetles and grasshoppers
Seeds and grasses
activities.explanation: Earthworms and millipedes may appear when the soil is wet after rain.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: Plant seeds remain in the soil
Rain falls or the seeds are watered
activities.explanation: Seeds can wait in soil. Rain or water helps them sprout.

activities.prompt: Which statement about soil life is correct?
options: Some insects emerge after rains.
Some insects die after rains.
All insects leave the soil.
Only seeds stay in soil.
activities.explanation: Some insects emerge from the soil after waiting for the rains.

activities.prompt: Old seeds are in soil. Rain falls. What will happen?
options: The seeds will sprout after the rain.
The seeds will turn into broken rocks.
The seeds will become small insects.
The seeds will stay dry and unchanged.

This mistake mixes seeds with the rock pieces in soil.
This mistake mixes sprouting with insects emerging from soil.
This mistake thinks seeds do not need rain or water.

activities.explanation: Rain lets the seeds sprout.

activities.prompt: How can a child fairly test if water helps seeds sprout?
options: Water one soil pot and leave the other dry.
Water both soil pots but use different seeds.
Water one soil pot but use different seeds.
Give water to two pots with different seeds.

why.Water both soil pots but use different s: Both water and seeds change, so no cause is clear.
why.Water one soil pot but use different see: The seeds change too, so water's effect is unclear.
why.Give water to two pots with different se: Both water and seeds change, so no cause is clear.

activities.explanation: Only water is changed, so its effect can be tested.

activities.prompt: No earthworm appears in wet soil after rain. What does this prove?
options: One check does not prove that no earthworms live there.
No earthworms can ever live in this soil.
Every earthworm left the soil before rain.
Earthworms can never appear after the rain.

why.No earthworms can ever live in this soil: This mistake treats one missing earthworm as proof that none live there.
why.Every earthworm left the soil before rai: This mistake thinks earthworms always leave before rain.
why.Earthworms can never appear after the ra: This mistake changes may appear into never appear.

activities.explanation: Earthworms may appear when soil is wet after rain.

lessons.title: How Animals Use Plants

activities.prompt: How do animals find food and make homes from plants?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Plants Help Animals
activities.body: Animals use plants in many ways. Camels eat leaves, while monkeys eat fruits. Caterpillars munch on leaves too. Sunbirds and butterflies drink nectar from flowers. Some animals use plants for homes. Owls use tree hollows. Squirrels and crows use twigs to build nests. Tailorbirds stitch leaves together to make their nests.
keyPoints: Animals eat leaves, fruits and nectar.
Owls use hollows in trees.
Some animals use plant parts to build nests.
activities.explanation: Plants can provide food and help animals build homes.

activities.prompt: In a garden, how do animals find both food and homes?
steps: Camels and caterpillars eat leaves, so leaves are food for them.
Monkeys eat fruit, and sunbirds and butterflies drink nectar.
Owls use hollows, while birds use twigs or stitched leaves for nests.
Animals use plants in different ways, not only as food.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose a Camel's Food
activities.prompt: Which plant part do camels eat?
options: fruits
leaves
nectar
twigs
activities.explanation: Good choice! Camels eat the leaves of plants.

activities.title: Caterpillar Food
activities.prompt: Caterpillars munch on ______ for food.
activities.hint: Caterpillars eat a plant part.
activities.explanation: Well done! Caterpillars munch on different leaves for food.

activities.title: Animal Plant Foods
activities.prompt: Match each animal to what it eats or drinks from plants.
activities.explanation: You matched each animal with its plant food.

activities.prompt: Monkeys eat the fruits of plants.
activities.explanation: Yes! Monkeys eat the fruits of plants.

activities.title: Plant Parts for Nests
activities.prompt: Match each animal group to the plant part it uses.
activities.explanation: You matched each group with the plant part it uses.

activities.title: Choose the Nest-Building Group
activities.prompt: Which animal group uses plant parts when making a nest?
options: Owls, squirrels, crows and monkeys
Camels, monkeys, sunbirds and owls
Caterpillars, butterflies, crows and monkeys
Owls, squirrels, crows and tailorbirds
activities.explanation: Well done! All these animals use parts of plants for nests.

activities.prompt: A hungry camel stands beside a plant with leaves and fruit. Which food will it choose?
options: Leaves, because camels eat plant leaves.
Fruit, because monkeys eat plant fruit.
Twigs, because squirrels and crows build nests.
Nectar, because sunbirds and butterflies drink it.

This mixes up camels with monkeys, which eat fruit.
why.Twigs, because squirrels and crows build: This mixes up camels with birds that use twigs for nests.
why.Nectar, because sunbirds and butterflies: This mixes up camels with animals that drink flower nectar.

activities.explanation: Right: camels eat the leaves of plants.

activities.prompt: A child says, “Animals use plants only for food.” Which event shows this claim is wrong?
options: An owl uses a tree hollow for its young.
A camel drinks nectar from a flower.
A monkey stitches leaves to build a nest.
A caterpillar carries twigs to build a nest.

Camels eat leaves, not flower nectar.
why.A monkey stitches leaves to build a nest: Monkeys eat fruit, but tailorbirds stitch leaf nests.
why.A caterpillar carries twigs to build a n: Caterpillars eat leaves, but squirrels and crows use twigs.

activities.explanation: Right: a tree hollow is a place, not food.

activities.prompt: A squirrel carries twigs toward a branch. Why does it do this?
options: To build a nest from plant twigs.
To stitch plant leaves into a nest.
To make a hollow for its young.
To munch on different leaves for food.

This confuses squirrels with tailorbirds, which stitch leaves.
This confuses squirrels with owls, which use tree hollows.
This confuses squirrels with caterpillars, which munch on leaves.

activities.explanation: Right: squirrels and crows use twigs to build nests.

activities.prompt: A monkey sees fruit growing on a plant. What will it most likely do?
options: Eat the fruit from the plant.
Eat the leaves of the plant.
Drink nectar from a flower.
Carry twigs to build a nest.

This confuses monkeys with camels and caterpillars, which eat leaves.
This confuses monkeys with sunbirds and butterflies, which drink nectar.
This confuses monkeys with squirrels and crows, which use twigs.

activities.explanation: Right: monkeys eat the fruits of plants.

activities.prompt: A sunbird and a butterfly visit different flowers that have nectar. What will they both do?
options: Drink the nectar from the flowers.
Eat the leaves of nearby plants.
Eat fruit hanging from the plants.
Build nests from twigs and leaves.

This confuses them with camels and caterpillars, which eat leaves.
This confuses them with monkeys, which eat fruit.
This confuses them with nest-building birds, which use twigs or leaves.

activities.explanation: Right: sunbirds and butterflies both drink flower nectar.

lessons.title: Listening to Birds

activities.prompt: Can you discover which birds are singing nearby?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Listen Carefully
activities.body: Different birds make different sounds. Close your eyes and listen carefully. Cup your ears with your hands. Point your face towards a sound. Work out which bird made it. Try making the sounds yourself. Write down sounds you hear. Compare them in the early morning, afternoon and evening. The bird table gives Gutru Gu and pigeon as examples.
keyPoints: Different birds make different sounds.
Close your eyes, cup your ears and listen.
Compare sounds in the early morning, afternoon and evening.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you listen closely and explore different bird sounds.

activities.prompt: You hear a bird outside. How can you work out which bird is making the sound?
steps: Close your eyes because each bird makes a different sound.
Cup your ears because this helps you focus on the call.
Point your face because the sound shows the direction.
Make the call and compare it to work out the bird.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Match the Actions
activities.prompt: Match each action to its detail.
activities.explanation: These pairs match the listening actions with their details.

activities.title: Write Down a Sound
activities.prompt: What should you write down after hearing a bird?
options: The colour of its feathers
The tree where it sat
The number of birds nearby
The sound it made
activities.explanation: Write down the sound of any birds you have heard.

activities.title: Compare Sounds
activities.prompt: Bird sounds should be compared only in the early morning.
activities.explanation: You compare bird sounds in the early morning, afternoon and evening.

activities.title: Order the Listening Times
activities.prompt: Put these times in order for comparing bird sounds.
activities.explanation: The bird sounds are compared from early morning to afternoon and evening.

activities.title: Bird Table Examples
activities.prompt: Which two examples are given on the bird table?
options: Early morning and pigeon
Gutru Gu and pigeon
Afternoon and Gutru Gu
Evening and bird sounds
activities.explanation: The bird table gives Gutru Gu and pigeon as examples.

activities.prompt: Your friend wants to hear a bird sound better. What should you do?
options: Cover your mouth and make the bird sound.
Write down the bird sound and stop listening.
Cup your ears with your hands and listen.
Point your face away from the sound.

why.Cover your mouth and make the bird sound: Covering your mouth takes your attention away from the bird.
why.Write down the bird sound and stop liste: Writing down the sound stops you from hearing it properly.
Facing away moves your attention away from the sound.

activities.explanation: Cupping your ears helps you focus on the bird sound.

activities.prompt: You hear Gutru Gu and pigeon calls. How can you tell them apart?
options: Choose by looking only at each bird's size.
Listen closely and try making each bird sound.
Write both calls as one long bird sound.
Point at both birds before listening to calls.

why.Choose by looking only at each bird's si: Looking only at size does not reveal which call you heard.
The two calls are different, not one long bird sound.
why.Point at both birds before listening to: Pointing before listening skips the careful sound check.

activities.explanation: Different birds make different sounds, so listening and copying help.

lessons.title: Reflecting and Watching a Caterpillar Change

activities.prompt: What happens when a caterpillar gets ready to fly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Looking closely and noticing change
activities.body: The reflection asks what soil is made of. It asks which animals, birds and insects you noticed around plants. You also recall how these creatures rely on plants. Suma observed a caterpillar for about 10 minutes. Her mother guided her to watch it each day. The caterpillar ate tender leaves continuously, then stopped eating. It formed a cocoon and came out as a butterfly. The butterfly flew away gently.
keyPoints: Reflection helps you notice soil, plants and nearby creatures.
Suma watched the caterpillar each day.
The caterpillar changed from a caterpillar into a butterfly.
activities.explanation: Careful observation helps you notice what is around you and how things change.

activities.prompt: What should you do when a caterpillar stops eating one day?
steps: Keep watching it each day, because the caterpillar may change again.
Look for a cocoon, because it formed after the caterpillar stopped eating.
Wait for it to come out, because a butterfly came out.
Expect it to fly away, because the butterfly flew away gently.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Suma's mother guide her to do each day?
options: Remember the plants she saw
Observe the caterpillar each day
Look for insects near plants
Recall how animals use plants
activities.explanation: Suma's mother guided her to observe the caterpillar each day.

activities.prompt: One day, the caterpillar stopped eating and formed a ______.
activities.hint: Use the word for what the caterpillar made.
activities.explanation: After stopping to eat, the caterpillar formed a cocoon.

activities.prompt: The caterpillar ate tender leaves continuously.
activities.explanation: The caterpillar was eating tender leaves continuously.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its matching answer.
pairs: What does the reflection ask about soil?
What does the reflection ask around plants?
which animals, birds and insects you noticed
What does the reflection ask you to recall about plants?
how animals, birds and insects rely on plants
activities.explanation: The reflection covers soil, nearby creatures and how they rely on plants.

activities.prompt: Put the caterpillar's change in the correct order.
items: It came out of the cocoon
activities.explanation: The caterpillar stopped eating, formed a cocoon, and later flew away as a butterfly.

activities.prompt: Which question does the reflection ask you to recall?
options: Which soil is around your plants?
How do animals, birds and insects rely on plants?
When did the butterfly fly away?
What did the caterpillar eat continuously?
activities.explanation: The reflection asks you to recall how animals, birds and insects rely on plants.

activities.prompt: A caterpillar is eating tender leaves. Then it stops. What comes next?
options: It keeps eating tender leaves.
It stays a caterpillar forever.
It forms a cocoon.
It flies away gently.

It had stopped eating, so eating more does not fit.
It later changed from a caterpillar into a butterfly.
It flew away only after becoming a butterfly.

activities.explanation: This is the next change after it stopped eating.

activities.prompt: Suma’s mother guides her to observe the caterpillar each day. Why is daily watching useful here?
options: It makes the caterpillar change faster each day.
It makes the caterpillar eat more each day.
It stops the caterpillar from forming a cocoon.
It lets her notice each change in the caterpillar.

why.It makes the caterpillar change faster e: The facts do not say that watching made it change faster.
why.It makes the caterpillar eat more each d: The facts do not say that watching made it eat more.
why.It stops the caterpillar from forming a: It formed a cocoon, so watching did not prevent that.

activities.explanation: Daily watching lets her see each change in the caterpillar.

activities.prompt: A child says, “The caterpillar formed a cocoon because it ate tender leaves.” What is wrong with this claim?
options: The facts show a sequence, but do not show its cause.
The caterpillar ate tender leaves after forming its cocoon.
The cocoon formed before the caterpillar stopped eating.
The butterfly formed the cocoon after flying away.

why.The caterpillar ate tender leaves after: It ate tender leaves before it stopped and formed the cocoon.
why.The cocoon formed before the caterpillar: It stopped eating before the cocoon formed.
why.The butterfly formed the cocoon after fl: The butterfly came out of the cocoon; it did not form it.

activities.explanation: The order is known, but the cause of the cocoon is not.

activities.context: During a visit to a garden, an elephant feeds on grass beside a tree. A caterpillar chews a leaf while a moth rests on another leaf. A colourful stink bug and a frog also rest on leaves, and a butterfly perches on one. Earthworms live on leaves and in the soil. Ants use leaves to build their nest, and a woodpecker sits on the tree trunk.
activities.prompt: What is most likely to happen to a leaf as a caterpillar chews it?
options: A chewed mark would appear in it.
Its edge would become smooth and unbroken.
It would stay unchanged because the caterpillar is only resting on it.
It would be carried away to become part of an ants' nest.

why.Its edge would become smooth and unbroke: Resting on a leaf does not make it smooth.
why.It would stay unchanged because the cate: The caterpillar is eating the leaf, not building with it.
why.It would be carried away to become part: The ant is the animal that uses leaves to build its nest.

activities.explanation: Chewing can damage the edge of a leaf.

activities.context: During a visit to a garden, an elephant feeds on grass beside a tree. A caterpillar chews a leaf while a moth rests on another leaf. A colourful stink bug and a frog also rest on leaves, and a butterfly perches on one. Earthworms live on leaves and in the soil. Ants use leaves to build their nest, and a woodpecker sits on the tree trunk.
activities.prompt: A student watches an ant bring a leaf toward the ants' nest. What should the student conclude?
options: The leaf will be used to help build the nest.
The leaf is food that the ant is about to eat.
The leaf is a temporary resting place for the ant.
The leaf will be used to block a caterpillar from the tree.

why.The leaf is food that the ant is about t: The ant is using the leaf as building material.
why.The leaf is a temporary resting place fo: Ants build with leaves rather than use them as beds.
why.The leaf will be used to block a caterpi: A caterpillar chews leaves rather than hide behind them.

activities.explanation: Ants use leaves when building their nest.

activities.prompt: Explain how animals use plants for food and as resting places.
activities.answer: Plants provide food and places for animals to rest. An elephant feeds on grass, while a caterpillar chews a leaf. A moth, a colourful stink bug, and a frog can rest on leaves, and a butterfly can perch on one. These animals gain food or a place to stay from the same kind of plant.
points: An elephant feeds on grass.
A caterpillar chews a leaf.
Moths, stink bugs, and frogs can rest on leaves.
A butterfly can perch on a leaf.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After rain, a student looked at the wet ground in a garden. The student saw an earthworm and a millipede on the soil. Nearby, an ant moved across the ground. The soil contained tiny pieces of broken rock, old plant parts, and living and dead animals. The student planted a seed and wondered whether it would sprout after being watered.
activities.prompt: What would happen next if the student watered the planted seed?
options: The seed would begin to grow.
The seed would stay in the soil and never sprout.
The seed would change into a tiny piece of broken rock.
The seed would change into an insect.

why.The seed would stay in the soil and neve: Seeds can remain in soil for long periods, but watering can cause sprouting.
why.The seed would change into a tiny piece: A seed grows into a plant rather than changing into broken rock.
A seed does not change into an insect.

activities.explanation: Watering can make a seed sprout, so growth would begin.

activities.context: After rain, a student looked at the wet ground in a garden. The student saw an earthworm and a millipede on the soil. Nearby, an ant moved across the ground. The soil contained tiny pieces of broken rock, old plant parts, and living and dead animals. The student planted a seed and wondered whether it would sprout after being watered.
activities.prompt: If a tiny creature is living in the soil, what should the student expect?
options: It may stay unseen even though it lives in the soil.
It must be visible because every soil creature can be seen.
It will change into a plant after the next rain.
It cannot be part of the soil unless it is dead.

why.It must be visible because every soil cr: This wrongly claims that every soil creature must be visible.
why.It will change into a plant after the ne: A tiny creature does not change into a plant after rain.
why.It cannot be part of the soil unless it: Living animals, as well as dead ones, can be part of soil.

activities.explanation: Some soil creatures are too small for people to see.

activities.prompt: Explain why soil is made of more than just tiny pieces of broken rock.
activities.answer: Soil has several parts. Tiny pieces of broken rocks help make it. Old leaves, roots, and stems are also part of it. Living and dead animals, including insects, are part of it. Many insects and other creatures live in the soil, and some are too small to see.
points: Tiny pieces of broken rocks help make soil.
Old leaves, roots, and stems are part of soil.
Living and dead animals, including insects, are part of soil.
Some soil creatures are too small to see.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a garden, caterpillars munch on different leaves, and sunbirds and butterflies drink nectar from different flowers. Monkeys eat plant fruits, while camels eat leaves. Tailorbirds stitch plant leaves to build nests, and squirrels and crows use twigs to build their nests. An owl uses a hollow in a tree to bring up its young. A gardener checks each nest and leaves suitable food for each animal.
activities.prompt: If the flowers in the garden were removed, what would happen next to the sunbirds and butterflies?
options: They would have no flower nectar to drink.
They would eat twigs instead.
They would live in a tree hollow.
They would munch on plant leaves.

Twigs are nest-building materials, not their food.
A tree hollow is used by an owl to bring up its young.
The case says these animals drink nectar rather than munch on leaves.

activities.explanation: Flowers provide the nectar that sunbirds and butterflies drink.

activities.context: In a garden, caterpillars munch on different leaves, and sunbirds and butterflies drink nectar from different flowers. Monkeys eat plant fruits, while camels eat leaves. Tailorbirds stitch plant leaves to build nests, and squirrels and crows use twigs to build their nests. An owl uses a hollow in a tree to bring up its young. A gardener checks each nest and leaves suitable food for each animal.
activities.prompt: The gardener finds a nest made from twigs. Which pair most likely built it?
options: The squirrel and the crow
The owl and the camel
The monkey and the butterfly
The sunbird and the caterpillar

why.The owl and the camel: Owls use tree hollows, while camels eat leaves.
why.The monkey and the butterfly: Monkeys eat fruits, while butterflies drink nectar.
why.The sunbird and the caterpillar: Sunbirds drink nectar, while caterpillars munch on leaves.

activities.explanation: Squirrels use twigs when building their nests.

activities.prompt: How do the animals in the case get food?
activities.answer: Caterpillars munch on leaves, and camels also eat leaves. Monkeys eat plant fruits, while sunbirds and butterflies drink nectar from flowers. These animals use different plant parts for food, so one garden can provide food for several kinds of animals.
points: Caterpillars and camels eat leaves.
Monkeys eat plant fruits.
Sunbirds and butterflies drink flower nectar.
Different animals use different plant parts for food.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the listening activity, a pupil hears a bird sound. The pupils close their eyes, cup their ears with their hands, and point their faces towards the sounds. The pupil works out which birds are making them and tries making those sounds. The pupil then writes down the sound of a bird heard and compares bird sounds in the early morning, afternoon and evening. The bird table gives Gutru Gu and pigeon as examples.
activities.prompt: The pupil hears a sound but still cannot tell which bird made it. What should happen next?
options: Continue listening and work out which bird is making the sound.
Cup the ears again and try making the sound.
Write down the sound and stop listening.
Compare the sound with sounds from another time of day.

why.Cup the ears again and try making the so: Making a sound is a later part of the activity.
The sound should be recorded after the listening activity.
why.Compare the sound with sounds from anoth: Comparing times comes after the initial bird-listening activity.

activities.explanation: This continues the bird-listening and identification step.

activities.context: During the listening activity, a pupil hears a bird sound. The pupils close their eyes, cup their ears with their hands, and point their faces towards the sounds. The pupil works out which birds are making them and tries making those sounds. The pupil then writes down the sound of a bird heard and compares bird sounds in the early morning, afternoon and evening. The bird table gives Gutru Gu and pigeon as examples.
activities.prompt: If the class visits in the early morning, afternoon and evening, what should it do?
options: Listen at each visit and compare what is heard.
Try making bird sounds at each visit and compare the attempts.
Record a sound at each visit but keep the lists separate.
Point towards sounds and identify birds at each visit.

why.Try making bird sounds at each visit and: Making sounds does not complete the time comparison.
why.Record a sound at each visit but keep th: Keeping lists separate misses the required comparison.
why.Point towards sounds and identify birds: Identifying birds at each visit does not compare the times.

activities.explanation: This completes the comparison between the different times.

activities.prompt: How should a pupil carry out the bird-listening activity from hearing a sound to recording it?
activities.answer: The pupil should close their eyes, cup their ears with their hands, and point their face towards each sound. The pupil should then work out which birds are making the sounds and try making those sounds. Finally, the pupil should write down the sound of a bird they have heard.
points: Close the eyes and cup the ears.
Point the face towards each sound.
Work out which birds are making the sounds.
Try making the sounds and record one heard.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Suma sat beside a plant and watched a caterpillar. Her mother guided her to observe it each day. Suma observed it for about 10 minutes. The caterpillar was eating tender leaves continuously. Her reflection asks what soil is made of, which animals, birds and insects she noticed around plants, and how they rely on plants. One day the caterpillar stopped eating and formed a cocoon. It came out as a butterfly and flew away gently.
activities.prompt: After Suma notices that the caterpillar has stopped eating, what should she reasonably expect to observe next?
options: The caterpillar will make a cocoon.
The caterpillar will begin eating again.
The caterpillar will fly away.
The caterpillar will turn into a cocoon.

The caterpillar continued eating until it stopped.
A new cocoon would form after the change.
The caterpillar did not fly; the butterfly did.

activities.explanation: This matches the order Suma observed.

activities.context: Suma sat beside a plant and watched a caterpillar. Her mother guided her to observe it each day. Suma observed it for about 10 minutes. The caterpillar was eating tender leaves continuously. Her reflection asks what soil is made of, which animals, birds and insects she noticed around plants, and how they rely on plants. One day the caterpillar stopped eating and formed a cocoon. It came out as a butterfly and flew away gently.
activities.prompt: Why is it useful for Suma to watch the caterpillar over several days instead of only once?
options: One observation may miss later stages in the insect's change.
One observation can show exactly what soil is made of.
Daily watching can make the caterpillar stop eating.
Several observations can show whether the butterfly stays nearby.

why.One observation can show exactly what so: Soil composition was not discovered by watching the caterpillar.
why.Daily watching can make the caterpillar: The change happened without daily watching causing it.
why.Several observations can show whether th: The butterfly flew away, so staying nearby was not shown.

activities.explanation: Suma saw different stages on different days.

activities.prompt: How is the caterpillar stage different from the butterfly stage in Suma's observation?
activities.answer: The caterpillar was the stage that ate tender leaves continuously. Later, it stopped eating and formed a cocoon. It then came out as a butterfly, and the butterfly flew away gently.
points: The caterpillar ate tender leaves.
It stopped eating and formed a cocoon.
It later came out as a butterfly.
The butterfly flew away gently.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Plants and Animals Live Together

activities.prompt: Which animal can rest on a leaf?
options: Frog
Elephant
Caterpillar
Woodpecker
activities.explanation: A frog can rest on a leaf. Elephants feed on grass.

activities.prompt: Soil is the topmost layer of the Earth's surface.
activities.explanation: Yes, soil is the topmost layer. This is the surface where plants can grow.

activities.prompt: Tiny pieces of ______ rocks help make soil.
activities.hint: These pieces come from rocks that have split.
activities.explanation: Broken rock pieces are one part of soil. Old plants and animals also belong to soil.

activities.prompt: Which group contains examples of insects?
options: Ants, termites, small beetles
Earthworms, millipedes, frogs
Camels, monkeys, owls
Squirrels, crows, sunbirds
activities.explanation: Ants, termites and small beetles are insects. Many insects live in soil.

activities.prompt: Put Suma's caterpillar observations in order.
items: The caterpillar ate tender leaves continuously
It came out as a butterfly
activities.explanation: Suma observed it for about 10 minutes. You followed each change in order.

activities.prompt: Which animal uses hollows in trees to bring up its young?
options: Owl
Camel
Monkey
Squirrel
activities.explanation: Owls use hollows in trees for their young. Other animals use plants in different ways.

activities.prompt: Seeds sprout when it rains or when they are watered.
activities.explanation: Yes, water helps seeds sprout. Some seeds can stay in soil for long periods.

activities.prompt: Match each bird or insect with its use of plants.
activities.explanation: Birds and insects use different plant parts. Your matching shows how they rely on plants.

activities.prompt: What should you point your face towards?
options: A bird sound
A green leaf
A tree trunk
A pile of soil
activities.explanation: Point towards the direction of a bird sound. Cup your ears to listen carefully.

chapters.title: Living in Harmony
chapters.summary: In this chapter: animals and plants in our homes; the mango tree; we need each other; get to know an animal.

lessons.title: Animals and Plants in Our Homes

activities.prompt: Which animals and plants might be sharing your home with you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sharing Our Homes
activities.body: We bring some animals and plants into our homes. Some have only just started living there. Sometimes they share our home happily. At other times, we do not like them there. We take care of some animals and plants by giving them water, food and shelter. We should not hurt animals, even when we dislike them or feel scared.
keyPoints: Some animals and plants live in our homes.
We give them water, food and shelter.
We should not hurt animals even when we dislike or fear them.
activities.explanation: The lesson reminds you to care for animals and plants kindly.

activities.prompt: An animal enters your home. You feel scared. What should you do?
steps: Do not hurt it, because animals should not be hurt when scared.
Animals usually do not hurt others unless we threaten them.
If it lives in your home, give it water, food and shelter.
Care for it without hurting it, even when you dislike it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where Do They Live?
activities.prompt: Where do some animals and plants live with us?
options: In our schools
At the market
In our homes
In a zoo
activities.explanation: We bring some animals and plants into our homes.

activities.title: What Do We Give?
activities.prompt: We give them water, food and ______.
activities.hint: This gives them a place to stay.
activities.explanation: We give animals and plants water, food and shelter.

activities.title: Why Do Animals Hurt Others?
activities.prompt: What makes animals usually hurt others?
options: They want more food
We upset them often
They feel threatened
They need fresh water
activities.explanation: Animals usually do not hurt others unless they feel threatened by us.

activities.title: Care Needs
activities.prompt: Match each need with what we give them.
activities.explanation: We give animals and plants water, food and shelter.

activities.title: Order the Care Needs
activities.prompt: Put the care needs in the order listed in your book.
activities.explanation: Your book lists water, food and shelter in that order.

activities.title: The Monkey in the Tree
activities.prompt: Where was the monkey in the example table seen?
options: on a road
inside a shop
in a tree
near a river
activities.explanation: The example table shows a monkey that was seen in a tree.

activities.prompt: An animal backs away when you reach it. What should you do?
options: Do not hurt it, because it may feel threatened by you.
Pull it closer, because scared animals need more space.
Chase it, because fear makes animals trust people.
Hurt it once, because scared animals need firm lessons.

why.Pull it closer, because scared animals n: This wrongly ignores that the animal may feel threatened.
why.Chase it, because fear makes animals tru: This wrongly thinks fear helps animals trust people.
why.Hurt it once, because scared animals nee: This wrongly treats fear as a reason to hurt animals.

activities.explanation: Right, because we should not hurt animals when we feel scared.

activities.prompt: One animal harms another. What is the fair conclusion?
options: Every animal harms others because animals always feel threatened.
No animal harms others because all animals live together happily.
Some animals harm others because they never feel threatened by us.
Animals usually do not harm others unless they feel threatened.

why.Every animal harms others because animal: This wrongly turns one harmful act into a rule about all animals.
why.No animal harms others because all anima: This wrongly turns one harmful act into a rule about none.
why.Some animals harm others because they ne: This wrongly says animals can never feel threatened by us.

activities.explanation: Right, because harm usually comes after animals feel threatened.

activities.prompt: A monkey was seen in a tree. What can we claim from this?
options: It was seen there, but this does not prove it lives inside.
It lives inside, because every monkey in a tree lives there.
It likes our home, because every monkey we see is happy.
We brought it home, because every monkey seen was brought inside.

why.It lives inside, because every monkey in: This wrongly assumes an animal in a tree lives inside.
why.It likes our home, because every monkey: This wrongly assumes every monkey we see is happy.
why.We brought it home, because every monkey: This wrongly assumes seeing an animal means we brought it home.

activities.explanation: Right, because seeing the monkey does not prove where it lives.

lessons.title: The Mango Tree

activities.prompt: What wonderful surprises can a mango tree share with us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Home in the Mango Tree
activities.body: Shambhu went through the forest with his father. They sat under the shade of a huge mango tree. The tree was home to birds, squirrels and monkeys. Shambhu saw a monkey eating a mango and throwing out the seed. A new plant will grow from that seed. This is how animals and plants help each other. We get many useful things from plants.
keyPoints: Shambhu and his father rest under a huge mango tree.
Birds, squirrels and monkeys have a home there.
A mango seed can grow into a new plant.
activities.explanation: The mango tree gives shade and a home, while its seed can become a new plant.

activities.prompt: Shambhu sits under a mango tree. How can this tree help people, animals, and a new plant?
steps: The tree gives Shambhu shade because plants can give us shade.
It gives birds, squirrels, and monkeys a home because it shelters animals.
The thrown seed can become a new plant because it can grow.
Animals help plants, and plants help animals, so they help each other.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did Shambhu and his father sit?
options: Under a huge mango tree
Under a small grey rock
Inside a bird's nest
Beside a wooden cart
activities.explanation: They rested under the shade of a huge mango tree.

activities.prompt: The mango tree was home to birds, squirrels and monkeys.
activities.explanation: All these animals had their home in the mango tree.

activities.prompt: The mango tree was home to birds, squirrels and ______.
activities.hint: This animal ate a mango.
activities.explanation: Monkeys lived in the mango tree and ate its mangoes.

activities.prompt: What did the monkey do with the mango?
options: Ate it and threw out the seed
Ate it and kept the seed
Dropped it and left the tree
Hid it under the tree
activities.explanation: Shambhu saw the monkey eat the mango and throw out its seed.

activities.prompt: Match each plant gift with its use.
activities.explanation: Plants give us shade and fibre for clothes. They also give us wood for building houses.

activities.prompt: We get only fruits from plants.
activities.explanation: Plants give us vegetables and many other things too. We also get medicine, fibre, wood and fresh air.

activities.prompt: Which sentence shows how animals and plants help each other?
options: A monkey drops a mango seed, and a new plant grows.
A bird drops a mango seed, and a new plant grows.
A monkey eats a mango, and a new house grows.
A squirrel throws a mango seed, and a new tree grows.
activities.explanation: The monkey throws out a mango seed, and a new plant grows from it. This helps animals and plants.

activities.prompt: Put the steps in order.
activities.explanation: The monkey eats the mango and throws out the seed. A new plant then grows from the seed.

activities.prompt: A monkey eats a mango and drops its seed. What can happen next?
options: A new plant will grow from the seed.
A new tree will grow from the monkey.
The mango will become a fresh plant.
The seed will grow into a house.

This confuses the seed with the animal that dropped it.
This confuses the mango fruit with its seed.
This confuses a living seed with wood used for houses.

activities.explanation: A new plant will grow from the thrown seed.

activities.prompt: A monkey throws out a mango seed. How does the monkey help a plant?
options: The monkey gives the plant fresh air.
The plant gives the monkey a house.
The seed can grow into a new plant.
The seed can turn into a bird.

This reverses the help because plants give animals fresh air.
This reverses the help between the monkey and the plant.
This confuses a seed with an animal that lives in trees.

activities.explanation: The thrown seed can grow into a new plant.

lessons.title: We Need Each Other

activities.prompt: How do animals, plants, and people help one another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Living Things Help Each Other
activities.body: Animals and plants need each other in many ways. They depend on each other for food and shelter. Animals help plants by dispersing seeds and making soil fertile. This helps plants grow and spread. We give care, protection, food and shelter to them. In return, we get lots of things from them. We treat them with kindness, care and compassion.
keyPoints: Animals and plants depend on each other.
Animals help plants grow and spread.
We treat animals and plants with kindness.
activities.explanation: Everything in nature can help something else, just as you help the world around you.

activities.prompt: We Need Each Other: A squirrel buries nuts in a park and forgets them. What might happen to trees there?
steps: Squirrels bury nuts and then forget where they hid them.
Some forgotten nuts can grow into trees.
This happens because animals can help plants spread their seeds.
So squirrels and plants need each other in surprising ways.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do squirrels do after burying nuts?
options: Forgets where they hid them.
Finds every nut again.
Plants them neatly in rows.
Keeps them safe from rain.
activities.explanation: Squirrels bury nuts and then forget where they hid them. This can help trees grow.

activities.prompt: Squirrels always remember where they hid their nuts.
activities.explanation: Squirrels forget where they hid their nuts. Their forgotten nuts can help new trees grow.

activities.prompt: Squirrels bury ______ and then forget where they hid them.
activities.hint: This is what squirrels hide.
activities.explanation: Good try. Squirrels bury nuts and then forget where they hid them.

activities.prompt: Animals and plants depend on each other only for food.
activities.explanation: They also depend on each other for shelter. Both needs help them stay balanced.

activities.prompt: We depend on plants and animals for food, shelter and clothing.
activities.explanation: Yes. Plants and animals give us food, shelter and clothing. That is why we need each other.

activities.prompt: Animals and plants depend on each other for which two needs?
options: Food and shelter.
Milk and clothing.
Care and compassion.
Protection and kindness.
activities.explanation: Animals and plants depend on each other for food and shelter. This helps them live together in balance.

activities.prompt: Animals help plants by dispersing seeds and making the soil ______.
activities.hint: This helps plants grow and spread.
activities.explanation: Exactly. Fertile soil helps plants grow and spread near and far.

activities.prompt: We Need Each Other: A squirrel buries nuts and forgets where. What may happen to trees?
options: Many trees may grow by accident.
The nuts may stay buried forever.
The nuts may turn into animals.
The trees may dry up quickly.

This mistake forgets that squirrels bury nuts and forget where.
This mistake mistakes nuts for animals, even though nuts can become trees.
This mistake thinks buried nuts stop trees from growing, which is not shown.

activities.explanation: This is right because forgotten nuts can grow into trees.

activities.prompt: Animals help plants by dispersing seeds and making soil fertile. Why is the claim “animals only harm plants” incomplete?
options: Animals also help plants grow and spread.
Animals never touch plants at all.
Plants harm every animal they meet.
Animals only make soil less fertile.

This mistake overlooks the help animals give plants.
This mistake reverses the relationship between animals and plants.
This mistake thinks animals always make soil less fertile.

activities.explanation: This is right because animals help plants grow and spread.

lessons.title: Get to Know an Animal

activities.prompt: Which animal nearby would you love to introduce to your class?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Observe and Describe
activities.body: Choose an animal or bird that you often see. You could choose a goat, cow, dog, cat, sparrow, parrot or duck. Observe it closely whenever you get a chance. Write a short description. Include when and where you first saw it. Say whether it was alone or with friends. Describe its sounds. Tell what surprised you or made you laugh. Then share your story.
keyPoints: Choose an animal or bird you often see.
Observe it closely and write a short description.
Share your story with your classmates.
activities.explanation: Looking closely helps you notice details for your story.

activities.prompt: You want to tell your class about an animal you often see.
steps: Choose an animal you often see, because then you can observe it.
Observe it closely whenever you can, because careful looking helps you learn.
Write about its first sighting and sounds, because observations help your description.
Share your story, because this is the final step with classmates.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose a Bird
activities.prompt: Which one is a bird you can choose?
options: cat
sparrow
goat
dog
activities.explanation: Great choice. A sparrow is a bird you can choose.

activities.title: Look Closely
activities.prompt: What should you do whenever you get a chance?
options: Feed it
Take it home
Observe it closely
Paint it
activities.explanation: Observing closely helps you notice details about your chosen animal.

activities.title: Write About It
activities.prompt: Write a short ______ of the animal or bird you chose.
activities.hint: This tells other people about your animal or bird.
activities.explanation: A description tells about the animal or bird you chose.

activities.title: Match the Examples
activities.prompt: Match each example with its description.
pairs: bird like a sparrow, parrot or duck
when and where you first saw it
whether it was alone or with its friends
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an animal or bird with a useful detail.

activities.title: Who Was There?
activities.prompt: Which sentence tells whether the animal had company?
options: It was alone.
It made a sound.
It surprised you.
You first saw it.
activities.explanation: This detail tells whether the animal was alone or with friends.

activities.title: Make Your Animal Story
activities.prompt: Put these actions in order.
activities.explanation: First, choose and observe. Then write and share your story.

activities.prompt: You often see a dog, but you have not observed it closely. What should you do next?
options: Choose the dog and watch it closely.
Choose the dog and write the story now.
Choose a parrot but never watch it.
Share a story before choosing an animal.

Writing before close observing may leave out important details.
Changing animals and refusing to observe avoids learning about your animal.
Sharing comes after you choose, observe, and write your story.

activities.explanation: This chooses an animal you often see and starts with observing it.

activities.prompt: A classmate says, "I can describe a cat well without watching it closely." Why is the claim weak?
options: Close observing helps you notice what your description needs.
Only birds need close observing, not animals like cats.
Choosing a cat already tells you every detail about it.
Sharing a story replaces the need to observe closely.

why.Only birds need close observing, not ani: Only birds need close observing, not animals like cats.
why.Choosing a cat already tells you every d: Choosing a cat already tells you every detail about it.
why.Sharing a story replaces the need to obs: Sharing a story replaces the need to observe closely.

activities.explanation: Close observing helps you notice what your description needs.

activities.prompt: You watched a parrot closely and heard a sound. What should your description include?
options: The sound the parrot made and what surprised you.
Only the place where you first saw the parrot.
The names of animals you did not choose.
The sounds of animals you never observed.

why.Only the place where you first saw the p: This gives the first place but leaves out the sound and surprise.
The description should be about the animal you chose.
why.The sounds of animals you never observed: This mixes sounds from other animals with your parrot's sound.

activities.explanation: This includes both the sound and the surprise from your observation.

lessons.title: Busy, Busy, Busy and Clever Ants!

activities.prompt: What might the ants choose first from three tasty treats?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Observe ants and care for plants
activities.body: Bring three small foods from your kitchen. Include one sweet food, one fried food, and one cooked food. Keep one foot of distance between them. Watch which food item the ants go to first. Not all ants may look the same. Talk to your plant when you feel sad, upset or angry. You can talk to it when happy. Plants and animals need care. We can help each other.
keyPoints: Bring small amounts of sweet, fried, and cooked food.
Keep one foot of distance between the foods.
Watch which food the ants choose first.
Talk to plants when you feel different emotions.
Plants and animals need our care.
activities.explanation: This helps you notice ant choices and show care for plants and animals.

activities.prompt: A child has sweet, fried, and cooked foods. How can the child learn which food ants go to first?
steps: Bring small amounts of three foods, because the child will watch them.
Keep the foods one foot apart, because each one must be watched.
Watch which food ants go to first, because this shows their choice.
The first food is the answer, even if the ants look different.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: One kind of food can be sweet, like sugar or jaggery.
activities.explanation: Sugar and jaggery are sweet foods. You can bring one for the ants.

activities.prompt: The sweet food can be like ______ or jaggery.
activities.hint: This food is sweet too.
activities.explanation: Sugar and jaggery are examples of sweet food.

activities.prompt: Which food is fried?
options: papad or murukku
sugar or jaggery
bread or idli
rice or ragi
activities.explanation: A papad or murukku is a fried food. The other foods are sweet or cooked.

activities.prompt: You cannot talk to your plant when you are happy.
activities.explanation: You can talk to your plant when you are happy. You can talk to it when upset too.

activities.prompt: Match each kind of food with an example.
pairs: bread, chapati, idli, rice or ragi
activities.explanation: Each food belongs to a kind: sweet, fried, or boiled or cooked.

activities.prompt: What should you watch during the ant activity?
options: the food item the ants go to first
the colour of your kitchen
the number of your fingers
the weather outside
activities.explanation: Watching the first food item shows which food the ants choose.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order for the ant activity.
items: Bring small amounts of three foods from your kitchen.
Keep one foot of distance between the three foods.
Watch which food item the ants go to first.
activities.explanation: Bring the foods, space them out, and then watch the ants.

activities.prompt: One food is sweet, one is fried, and one is cooked. How should the child place the foods?
options: Keep the three foods one foot apart.
Put the three foods in one pile.
Keep the three foods very close.
Keep just one food for the ants.

A pile makes it hard to see which food ants go to first.
Very close foods make it hard to see which food comes first.
One food cannot show a fair choice among three kinds.

activities.explanation: This gives each food equal space, so the test is fair.

activities.prompt: A child says, "All ants at these foods will look the same." What is the fair reply?
options: Not all the ants may look the same.
All the ants here must look the same.
Only ants at sweet food may look different.
Every ant here must have a different look.

This repeats the claim without checking how ants may look.
why.Only ants at sweet food may look differe: Nothing says that only sweet food has different-looking ants.
why.Every ant here must have a different loo: This changes one wrong idea into another wrong idea.

activities.explanation: This is fair because ants do not all need to look alike.

lessons.title: Guessing Games, Reflection and a True Story

activities.prompt: How can we discover the animals and plants that share our world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Games and the World Around Us
activities.body: You can play a guessing game by acting like an animal. Your partner guesses which animal you are, and you can switch roles. People, plants and animals depend on each other. You can name a favourite animal, bird, insect or plant. Later, read a true story about children watching birds in Valparai, Tamil Nadu.
keyPoints: Act like an animal so your partner can guess.
People, plants and animals depend on each other.
Valparai has a true story about visiting birds.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the animal game and the true bird story.

activities.prompt: Your partner acts and moves like an animal. How can the class play?
steps: Watch the acting, because it gives clues about the animal.
Watch the movements, because they give more clues.
Make a guess, because the class has to guess the animal.
After guessing, switch roles because you can try both parts.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Guess the Animal
activities.prompt: What does the class have to guess during the animal game?
options: which animal it is
who should act first
where to switch roles
how many roles to use
activities.explanation: The partner acts like an animal. The class guesses the animal.

activities.prompt: You can switch roles after the guessing game.
activities.explanation: The lesson says you can switch roles after the game.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each word or group with the correct information.
pairs: a small town in Tamil Nadu
activities.explanation: The pairs show mutual dependence and details from the true story.

activities.title: Where Do the Birds Come From?
activities.prompt: Grey Wagtails arrive all the way from the ______.
activities.hint: Think of where the birds travel from.
activities.explanation: Grey Wagtails come all the way from the mountains.

activities.title: Your Favourite
activities.prompt: What can you name for this lesson?
options: Your favourite animal, bird, insect or plant.
Your favourite guessing role.
Your favourite town game.
Your favourite welcome poster.
activities.explanation: You can name any favourite animal, bird, insect or plant.

activities.title: The True Bird Story
activities.prompt: In the true story, what do the children and teachers do?
options: They look for and record town birds.
They sell the town's birds.
They keep the birds at home.
They name the town's shops.
activities.explanation: The children and teachers look for and record birds that visit their town.

activities.title: Welcome Posters
activities.prompt: What do they put up when the birds arrive?
options: posters about the town's shops
posters for the teachers
posters about the mountains
welcome posters for the birds
activities.explanation: They put up welcome posters when the birds arrive.

activities.prompt: Grey Wagtails are commonly known as Vaalatti kuruvi in Tamil.
activities.explanation: This is the common Tamil name for Grey Wagtails.

activities.prompt: A child says animals do not need us. Why is that wrong?
options: People and plants and animals depend on each other.
Plants and animals depend on us, but people do not need them.
People depend on plants and animals, but they do not need us.
Plants and animals depend on nobody at all.

why.Plants and animals depend on us, but peo: This mistakes one-way dependence for the two-way relationship we have.
why.People depend on plants and animals, but: This forgets that plants and animals also depend on us.
why.Plants and animals depend on nobody at a: This thinks dependence never goes from plants and animals to people.

activities.explanation: This is right because people need plants and animals, and they need us.

activities.prompt: Grey Wagtails come from mountains. Why is saying they never travel wrong?
options: Grey Wagtails, called Vaalatti kuruvi, reach Valparai.
Grey Wagtails never reach Valparai or any town.
Grey Wagtails are insects, not travelling birds.
Vaalatti kuruvi are garden plants, not birds.

why.Grey Wagtails never reach Valparai or an: This wrongly thinks the birds never visit towns like Valparai.
why.Grey Wagtails are insects, not travellin: This mistakes travelling birds for insects.
why.Vaalatti kuruvi are garden plants, not b: This mistakes a bird's common name for the name of a plant.

activities.explanation: This is right because these Vaalatti kuruvi reach Valparai from the mountains.

lessons.sceneAlt: Yellow and blue fish swim together in a home aquarium.
