lessons.title: Why we drink water

activities.prompt: Why does our body need water on hot summer days?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why water matters in summer
activities.body: Summer is very hot, so we sweat a lot. Sweating makes us lose water from our body. That is why we need to drink water frequently. In summer we drink more water, buttermilk and lime water. We can also drink aam panna, sugarcane juice or tender coconut water. Our body needs a lot of water. We cannot live without water.
keyPoints: Summer is hot and we sweat a lot
Sweating makes us lose water from our body
Our body needs a lot of water
activities.explanation: This lesson shows why water matters so much in summer.

activities.prompt: It is hot in summer. After playing, the child sweats. What should the child do, and why?
steps: The hot summer weather makes us sweat a lot.
Sweating takes water out of our body.
Our body needs a lot of water.
So we should drink water frequently, especially after sweating.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In summer, which drinks do we have more of?
options: Milk and yoghurt
Tea and coffee
Juice and milk shakes
Water, buttermilk and lime water
activities.explanation: Yes! In summer we drink more water, buttermilk and lime water.

activities.prompt: It is very hot in summer, so we ______ a lot.
activities.hint: You do this when your body gets hot.
activities.explanation: Good try! We sweat a lot in summer, and that water has to be replaced.

activities.prompt: Why should we drink water frequently?
options: Because water is very sweet
Because our body needs a lot of water
Because sweat makes us feel heavy
Because it cools the food we eat
activities.explanation: Right! Our body needs a lot of water, and we cannot live without it.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its partner.
pairs: We lose water from our body
Aam panna, sugarcane juice, tender coconut water
activities.explanation: You matched them all! Summer and games both make us sweat and lose water.

activities.prompt: Put these in the order they happen when you play in summer.
items: You play and your body gets hot
activities.explanation: Well done! Playing makes us sweat, sweating takes water away, and then we drink.

activities.prompt: Why does our body need so much water?
options: To help us sleep at night
To make our body lose water
Because our body needs a lot of it
To keep our hands and feet warm
activities.explanation: Exactly right! Our body needs a lot of water, and we cannot live without it.

activities.prompt: In hot summer, a child starts sweating. What happens next?
options: The child will gain water in the body.
The child will lose water from the body.
The child will need much less water.
The child will sweat much less.

This reverses sweating's effect on body water.
Losing water means needing water, not less.
Hot summer makes us sweat more, not less.

activities.explanation: Sweating makes water leave the body.

activities.prompt: A child plays and sweats during the activity. Why should the child drink water afterward?
options: Playing adds water to the body.
The body needs water only on hot days.
Playing makes the body lose water through sweat.
Sweat contains no water from the body.

This confuses water loss with water gain.
This wrongly limits water needs to hot days.
Sweat is water lost from the body.

activities.explanation: Sweating during play makes the body lose water.

activities.prompt: We also sweat when we play. Which comparison can fairly test this idea?
options: Children playing with children playing.
Children resting with children resting.
Children playing with children sleeping.
Children playing with children resting.

This compares playing with playing, so it cannot test the idea.
This has no playing child for comparison.
Sleeping still does not provide a playing comparison.

activities.explanation: It compares playing with not playing.

activities.prompt: We sweat a lot in hot summer. A child says, "I will not lose water unless I play." What is wrong?
options: Only playing can make the body lose water.
Hot summer sweat can also make the body lose water.
Hot summer weather makes the body gain water.
Water leaves the body only during physical activity.

why.Only playing can make the body lose wate: This wrongly says summer sweating cannot remove water.
why.Hot summer weather makes the body gain w: This reverses what sweating does to body water.
why.Water leaves the body only during physic: This wrongly limits water loss to physical activity.

activities.explanation: Summer sweating can remove water even without play.

activities.prompt: In summer, we sweat a lot and lose body water. Which choice follows the lesson best?
options: Drink less water, buttermilk, or lime water.
Drink only buttermilk, and never drink water.
Drink more water, buttermilk, or lime water.
Drink nothing while sweating in summer.

why.Drink less water, buttermilk, or lime wa: This mistakes water loss for needing fewer drinks.
why.Drink only buttermilk, and never drink w: This wrongly says summer water is not useful.
Sweating removes water, so drinking nothing is wrong.

activities.explanation: These drinks are suggested when summer sweating loses water.

activities.prompt: A person cannot drink water. We cannot live without water. What must be true?
options: The person's body will not need water.
The person's body will need much less water.
The person can live normally without water.
The person cannot keep living without water.

This confuses having no water with not needing it.
why.The person's body will need much less wa: A water shortage does not reduce the body's need.
why.The person can live normally without wat: This wrongly says water is not needed for life.

activities.explanation: Life cannot continue without water.

lessons.title: Food from plants and animals

activities.prompt: Where do the foods on our plates begin?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where our food comes from
activities.body: We eat different parts of plants. Spinach, fenugreek, cabbage, mustard and coriander are leafy foods. Guava, sapota, apple and mango are fruits. Carrot, radish and beetroot are roots. Potatoes, bamboo shoots, ginger and onion are listed as stems. Seeds, grains, pulses and dry fruits are also plant foods. Some people eat animal foods too.
keyPoints: Plants give us leaves, fruits, roots and stems.
Seeds, grains, pulses and dry fruits are plant foods.
Some foods come from animals.
activities.explanation: Food comes from many different parts of plants and from animals.

activities.prompt: How can we sort spinach, carrot, mango, and milk?
steps: Spinach is a leaf food, and carrot is a root food.
Mango is a fruit food, while milk comes from an animal.
So spinach, carrot, and mango are plant foods, but milk is not.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose a leafy food
activities.prompt: Which food is listed under leaves?
options: Spinach
Carrot
Mango
Potato
activities.explanation: Spinach is listed among the leafy foods.

activities.title: Choose a root food
activities.prompt: Which food is listed as a root?
options: Carrot
Cabbage
Sapota
Honey
activities.explanation: Carrot is listed among the root foods.

activities.title: A food from stems
activities.prompt: Potatoes are listed under ______.
activities.hint: Which plant part gives us potatoes?
activities.explanation: Potatoes, bamboo shoots, ginger and onion are listed as stems.

activities.title: Match the food to its group
activities.prompt: Match each food to the group where it is listed.
activities.explanation: Each food belongs to a different plant group.

activities.title: Order the plant-food groups
activities.prompt: Put these food groups in the order shown in your book.
items: seeds, grains, pulses and dry fruits
activities.explanation: Your book lists leaves, fruits, roots, stems and other plant foods in this order.

activities.title: Choose animal foods
activities.prompt: Which pair contains foods that come from animals?
options: Cheese and honey
Spinach and cabbage
Carrot and beetroot
Mango and sapota
activities.explanation: Cheese and honey both come from animals.

activities.prompt: A cook sorts spinach, coriander, carrot, and mango. Which pair belongs together?
options: Spinach and coriander
Carrot and mango
Spinach and carrot
Coriander and mango

why.Carrot and mango: Carrot is a root, while mango is a fruit.
why.Spinach and carrot: Spinach is a leaf, while carrot is a root.
why.Coriander and mango: Coriander is a leaf, while mango is a fruit.

activities.explanation: Spinach and coriander are both listed as leafy foods.

activities.prompt: A plate has milk, paneer, honey, and mango. How many foods come from animals?
options: One food
Two foods
Three foods
Four foods

why.One food: This forgets that milk, paneer, and honey come from animals.
why.Two foods: This counts only one of the three animal foods.
why.Four foods: This wrongly counts mango as food from an animal.

activities.explanation: Milk, paneer, and honey all come from animals.

activities.prompt: A shop labels seeds, grains, pulses, and dry fruits as fruits. What is the best reply?
options: They are other listed plant foods.
They are listed as root foods.
They are listed as stem foods.
They are listed as animal foods.

Roots are carrot, radish, and beetroot, not this group.
Stems are potatoes, bamboo shoots, ginger, and onion.
These are plant foods, not foods from animals.

activities.explanation: These are other listed plant foods, not fruits.

activities.prompt: Apple and mango are fruits. A child says all plant foods are fruits. Which pair should be checked next?
options: Spinach and carrot
Curd and paneer
Milk and honey
Apple and sapota

why.Curd and paneer: Curd and paneer come from animals, so they cannot check plant foods.
why.Milk and honey: Milk and honey come from animals, so they cannot check plant foods.
why.Apple and sapota: Apple and sapota are both fruits, so this checks no other plant parts.

activities.explanation: Spinach and carrot are plant foods from leaves and roots.

activities.context: At a festival, a family prepared chhappan bhog for guests, friends and family. The meal had 56 varieties of food, and the foods together gave a good mixture of six tastes: sweet, spicy, astringent, sour, salty and bitter. The family also served fruit, vegetables, rice, dal, roti, milk, lassi and juice.
activities.prompt: The host notices that the meal includes sweet and sour foods but wants the full mixture of tastes. What should the host do?
options: Add foods with the other tastes so all six are represented.
Add only more sweet foods because one taste is enough.
Add only more sour foods because two tastes are enough.
Remove the varied foods and serve one sweet item.

why.Add only more sweet foods because one ta: One taste would not make a six-taste mixture.
why.Add only more sour foods because two tas: Two tastes would still leave several tastes out.
why.Remove the varied foods and serve one sw: Removing the variety would lose the full mixture of tastes.

activities.explanation: This would include all six tastes.

activities.context: At a festival, a family prepared chhappan bhog for guests, friends and family. The meal had 56 varieties of food, and the foods together gave a good mixture of six tastes: sweet, spicy, astringent, sour, salty and bitter. The family also served fruit, vegetables, rice, dal, roti, milk, lassi and juice.
activities.prompt: If the family replaced the varied foods with foods having only sweet and sour tastes, what would happen?
options: Four of the tastes would be missing from the food.
All six tastes would still be represented.
Only the salty taste would be missing.
The other four tastes would become stronger.

why.All six tastes would still be represente: The other four tastes would still be absent.
Spicy, astringent and bitter would also be missing.
why.The other four tastes would become stron: Tastes that are absent cannot become stronger.

activities.explanation: Sweet and sour would replace four of the six tastes.

activities.prompt: Explain why one person might choose sweet food while another chooses sour food.
activities.answer: Sweet and sour are two different tastes. Some food items are sweet, while others are sour. People enjoy different kinds of food and drink, so one person may like sweet food and another may prefer sour food.
points: Sweet and sour are different tastes.
Some foods are sweet and others are sour.
People enjoy different kinds of food and drink.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Shirin ran faster than everyone in her class. She met a champion with many medals, who said she could become a champion if she practised a lot and ate healthy food. Shirin practised a lot but often fell sick. She ate rice and potatoes, different vegetables and fruits, foods made from grains, pulses or dal, and nuts. She also ate food cooked at home. After a few months, Shirin ran faster than before.
activities.prompt: Why did the champion tell Shirin to eat many other foods as well?
options: Many kinds of food helped build a strong, healthy body.
Rice and potatoes were not good foods for Shirin.
She had to stop practising before eating other foods.
Different foods could replace practising a lot.

why.Rice and potatoes were not good foods fo: The champion said rice and potatoes were good for Shirin.
why.She had to stop practising before eating: The champion encouraged both practice and healthy food.
why.Different foods could replace practising: Different foods support healthy eating; they do not replace practice.

activities.explanation: This matches the champion's advice and Shirin's later improvement.

activities.context: Shirin ran faster than everyone in her class. She met a champion with many medals, who said she could become a champion if she practised a lot and ate healthy food. Shirin practised a lot but often fell sick. She ate rice and potatoes, different vegetables and fruits, foods made from grains, pulses or dal, and nuts. She also ate food cooked at home. After a few months, Shirin ran faster than before.
activities.prompt: Why did Shirin's running improve after a few months?
options: She practised a lot and ate varied healthy food.
She stopped falling sick before she began to practise.
The champion ran faster than everyone in her class.
She ate only rice and potatoes while she was ill.

why.She stopped falling sick before she bega: She often fell sick while practising, before changing her food.
why.The champion ran faster than everyone in: The champion was not part of Shirin's class.
why.She ate only rice and potatoes while she: She needed many foods as well, not only rice and potatoes.

activities.explanation: Shirin combined plenty of practice with varied healthy food.

activities.context: Shirin ran faster than everyone in her class. She met a champion with many medals, who said she could become a champion if she practised a lot and ate healthy food. Shirin practised a lot but often fell sick. She ate rice and potatoes, different vegetables and fruits, foods made from grains, pulses or dal, and nuts. She also ate food cooked at home. After a few months, Shirin ran faster than before.
activities.prompt: If Shirin forgot pulses and nuts, what should she do next?
options: Include pulses and nuts among her other foods.
Eat only vegetables and fruits instead.
Stop eating food cooked at home.
Keep forgetting them because they do not matter.

She was told to eat many different foods, not fewer kinds.
Food cooked at home was also good for Shirin.
why.Keep forgetting them because they do not: Pulses and nuts were foods she was told to eat.

activities.explanation: Pulses and nuts were part of Shirin's healthy food.

activities.prompt: Explain how Shirin could work towards becoming a champion.
activities.answer: Shirin should keep practising and eat healthy food. She can choose rice and potatoes, different vegetables and fruits, foods made from grains, pulses or dal, and nuts. Food cooked at home is also good for her. These choices helped her have a strong and healthy body and run faster.
points: Practises a lot
Eats different vegetables and fruits
Includes grains, pulses or dal, and nuts
Eats food cooked at home
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a hot summer day, a family goes for a picnic with friends. They take ice-cream and tender coconut water because the weather is hot. At the picnic, they find mangoes and melons. One friend says that people staying in another part of the country may eat foods different from theirs. The family wonders what people might enjoy during a cold winter day.
activities.prompt: If the picnic day changed to a cold winter day, which choice would best match the foods people enjoy in winter?
options: Warm foods, soups and stews
Ice-cream and kulfi
Tender coconut water
Mangoes and melons

why.Ice-cream and kulfi: Ice-cream and kulfi are enjoyed when it is hot.
why.Tender coconut water: Tender coconut water is enjoyed in summer.
why.Mangoes and melons: Mangoes and melons are available in summer.

activities.explanation: Warm foods, soups and stews are winter choices.

activities.context: During a hot summer day, a family goes for a picnic with friends. They take ice-cream and tender coconut water because the weather is hot. At the picnic, they find mangoes and melons. One friend says that people staying in another part of the country may eat foods different from theirs. The family wonders what people might enjoy during a cold winter day.
activities.prompt: The friends later travel to another part of the country. What might they discover?
options: They may find foods different from the foods they usually eat.
They must eat exactly the same foods they eat at home.
They will find only mangoes and melons wherever they go.
They will find no foods different from their usual foods.

why.They must eat exactly the same foods the: Travelers may find foods different from their usual foods.
why.They will find only mangoes and melons w: Mangoes and melons are not the only foods found while traveling.
why.They will find no foods different from t: Different places can have foods that are different from ours.

activities.explanation: People in another part of the country may eat different foods.

activities.prompt: Explain why the foods and drinks in the case suit a hot summer day.
activities.answer: In hot weather, the family may choose kulfi or ice-cream because these are foods people love to eat when it is hot. Tender coconut water is also a drink they enjoy in summer. These choices suit the season shown in the case.
points: Kulfi and ice-cream suit hot weather.
Tender coconut water is enjoyed in summer.
The choices match the hot season in the case.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: It is summer, and the weather is hot. A child is playing and sweats a lot. This sweating makes the child lose water from the body. The family gives the child water, and the child can also have buttermilk or lime water. After the activity, the child should keep drinking water frequently because the body needs a lot of water and cannot live without it.
activities.prompt: If the child does not drink after sweating during play, what will happen?
options: The body will be short of needed water.
The body will lose even more water while sitting still.
The body will need less water after the play.
The child will no longer need any drinks.

why.The body will lose even more water while: Being still does not undo the water that was lost.
why.The body will need less water after the: Playing does not reduce the body's need for water.
why.The child will no longer need any drinks: The body always needs water to live.

activities.explanation: Sweating has already made the body lose water.

activities.context: It is summer, and the weather is hot. A child is playing and sweats a lot. This sweating makes the child lose water from the body. The family gives the child water, and the child can also have buttermilk or lime water. After the activity, the child should keep drinking water frequently because the body needs a lot of water and cannot live without it.
activities.prompt: What should the child do during and after the physical activity?
options: Keep taking water regularly during and after the play.
Stop drinking as soon as the play ends.
Drink less because the body has already sweated.
Drink water only before the activity begins.

Water is still needed after the activity ends.
why.Drink less because the body has already: Water already lost through sweat must be replaced.
why.Drink water only before the activity beg: Drinking only before playing does not meet the need for frequent water.

activities.explanation: Water should be taken frequently, including after activity.

activities.prompt: How are sweating in summer and sweating during physical activity alike, and what should we do?
activities.answer: Summer heat and physical activity both make us sweat. Sweating takes water out of our body. We should therefore drink water often, especially during summer and after playing, because the body needs a lot of water.
points: Summer heat is linked with sweating.
Physical activity also causes sweating.
Sweating removes water from the body.
Water should be drunk frequently.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A family is sorting ingredients for a meal. Spinach and coriander are in one basket, carrot and beetroot in another, apple and mango in a third, and potato, ginger and onion in a fourth. They also have milk, curd, cheese, honey, eggs and meat in another basket. The family wants to label every basket by the plant part or animal source it represents.
activities.prompt: If spinach and carrot are accidentally placed in the same basket, how should the family correct the mistake?
options: Move carrot to the root basket and spinach to the leafy basket.
Move both foods to the fruit basket.
Move spinach to the root basket and carrot to the leafy basket.
Move both foods to the animal-food basket.

Spinach and carrot are not listed as fruits.
why.Move both foods to the animal-food baske: They are listed as plant foods, not animal foods.

activities.explanation: This matches the listed leaf and root groups.

activities.context: A family is sorting ingredients for a meal. Spinach and coriander are in one basket, carrot and beetroot in another, apple and mango in a third, and potato, ginger and onion in a fourth. They also have milk, curd, cheese, honey, eggs and meat in another basket. The family wants to label every basket by the plant part or animal source it represents.
activities.prompt: If curd is removed from the animal-food basket and paneer is added, what would happen?
options: The basket would still contain animal foods because paneer comes from animals.
The basket would become a fruit group because paneer is listed as a fruit.
The basket would become a plant group because paneer comes from a plant.
The basket would become a stem group because paneer is listed with potatoes.

why.The basket would become a fruit group be: Paneer is not listed as a fruit.
why.The basket would become a plant group be: Paneer comes from animals, not plants.
why.The basket would become a stem group bec: Paneer is not listed under stems.

activities.explanation: Paneer comes from animals, so it fits the animal-food group.

activities.context: A family is sorting ingredients for a meal. Spinach and coriander are in one basket, carrot and beetroot in another, apple and mango in a third, and potato, ginger and onion in a fourth. They also have milk, curd, cheese, honey, eggs and meat in another basket. The family wants to label every basket by the plant part or animal source it represents.
activities.prompt: The family chooses apple, ginger, honey and onion for another basket. Which set of labels is correct?
options: Apple—fruit; ginger—stem; honey—animal source; onion—stem.
Apple—fruit; ginger—root; honey—animal source; onion—stem.
Apple—stem; ginger—fruit; honey—animal source; onion—root.
Apple—fruit; ginger—stem; honey—plant stem; onion—fruit.

why.Apple—fruit; ginger—root; honey—animal s: Ginger is listed under stems, not roots.
why.Apple—stem; ginger—fruit; honey—animal s: Apple is a fruit and ginger is a stem.
why.Apple—fruit; ginger—stem; honey—plant st: Honey comes from animals, while onion is a stem.

activities.explanation: It correctly identifies every food's listed group.

activities.prompt: Explain why spinach and carrot should be placed in different groups even though both are foods from plants.
activities.answer: Spinach is listed under leaves, while carrot is listed under roots. The family groups plant foods by the part they come from, so putting them in separate groups helps show that spinach and carrot come from different plant parts.
points: Spinach is listed under leaves.
Carrot is listed under roots.
Different plant parts belong to different groups.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

options: Special festival food
Sports training food

activities.prompt: Rice and ______ were good foods for Shirin.

options: Mangoes
Melons
Apples
Coconut water

activities.prompt: Sweating makes our body lose water.

activities.prompt: Put Shirin's story events in order.
items: She ran faster than everyone in her class.
She practised a lot but often fell sick.
After a few months, she ran faster than before.

activities.prompt: Put the summer water-loss events in order.
items: You play or do physical activity.
activities.explanation: Physical activity makes us sweat. Sweating makes us lose water, so we should drink water frequently.

activities.prompt: Match each food to its category.

lessons.title: Clean and Bright: Daily Habits

activities.prompt: What are the little daily habits that keep us clean and bright?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Clean and Bright Habits
activities.body: Clean and bright habits help your body stay clean and free from diseases. Brush your teeth every day. Take a shower and comb your hair to keep it tidy. Wash your hands with soap, especially after using the toilet or returning from outdoors. Trim and clean your nails. Drink 6–8 glasses of water and sleep for at least eight hours. Rinse your mouth after eating.
keyPoints: Daily habits help keep our bodies clean and free from diseases.
Brush, shower, comb, wash, trim, rinse, drink, and sleep.
Some daily activities are done more than once.
activities.explanation: These good habits help you stay clean, healthy, and bright.

activities.prompt: A child returns from outside, eats a snack, and brushes their teeth. What should the child do to stay clean?
steps: First, they should wash their hands with soap because they returned from outdoors.
Next, they should rinse their mouth because they ate food.
They should brush their teeth every day because good habits help keep bodies clean.
So, handwashing, rinsing, and brushing help keep their body clean.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Clean Hands
activities.prompt: Which habit helps keep your hands clean?
options: Brushing teeth
Washing with soap
Combing hair
Trimming nails
activities.explanation: Washing your hands with soap helps keep your body clean.

activities.prompt: We should comb our hair to keep it tidy.
activities.explanation: Combing your hair helps keep it tidy. It is a good daily habit.

activities.title: The Right Cleaner
activities.prompt: Wash your hands with ______.
activities.hint: What should you use when washing your hands?
activities.explanation: Soap helps you wash your hands properly and keep them clean.

activities.title: Match Each Habit
activities.prompt: Match each body part to its good habit.
activities.explanation: Each body part has a good habit that helps keep it clean and tidy.

activities.title: When to Wash
activities.prompt: When should you wash your hands with soap?
options: After using the toilet
Only before sleeping
After combing hair
Only after eating
activities.explanation: Wash with soap after using the toilet and returning from outdoors.

activities.title: Why Wash Hands?
activities.prompt: Why should you wash your hands with soap after returning from outdoors?
options: It keeps your body clean
It helps you sleep well
It replaces brushing
It keeps your hair tidy
activities.explanation: Washing with soap helps keep your body clean. It is important after returning from outdoors.

activities.prompt: We should sleep for less than eight hours altogether.
activities.explanation: We should sleep well for at least eight hours altogether. Good habits help keep our bodies free from diseases.

activities.title: Choose Good Habits
activities.prompt: A child wants clean, bright daily habits. Which choice matches the lesson?
options: Brush and shower daily
Comb hair very seldom
Trim nails and stop
Skip washing hands
activities.explanation: Brushing every day, showering, and washing with soap are good daily habits.

activities.prompt: A child uses the toilet and plays outside. How should they wash?
options: Wash with soap after both times.
Wash only after toilet use.
Wash only after returning outdoors.
Wash before both times.

This forgets washing after returning from outdoors.
This forgets washing after using the toilet.
The habit says to wash after both times.

activities.explanation: Soap washing is needed after both times.

lessons.title: Cleaning Our Teeth in Different Ways

activities.prompt: How did people keep their teeth clean before toothbrushes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Ways to Clean
activities.body: People have different ways of keeping their teeth clean. Dadu chews neem or babool twigs to make brushes. This method is called datun. Datun means using twigs of certain plants to clean teeth. Karanj is another plant used for datun. Modern brushing came from an Indian hygiene tradition. Reetha and Shikakai can clean hair naturally. Some traditional methods also use safe and effective household cleaning recipes.
keyPoints: Dadu uses neem or babool twigs to clean his teeth.
Datun means using twigs of certain plants to clean teeth.
Traditional methods can clean teeth, hair and homes.
activities.explanation: This lesson explores natural and modern ways of cleaning.

activities.prompt: Dadu wants to clean his teeth with a plant twig. What should he do, and why?
steps: Dadu should get a fresh twig from nearby trees each day, because he uses one daily.
He can choose neem or babool, because datun uses twigs of certain plants.
He should chew the twig, because chewing turns it into a brush.
Then he can rub his teeth, because the twig removes stuck food and massages his gums.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Dadu's Choice
activities.prompt: What does Dadu use to clean his teeth?
options: Neem or babool twigs
Reetha or Shikakai
Karanj or Reetha
Neem or Karanj
activities.explanation: Dadu uses neem or babool twigs to clean his teeth.

activities.title: The Bitter Twig
activities.prompt: Moyna found the ______ twig very bitter.
activities.hint: This plant can be used for datun.
activities.explanation: Moyna found the neem twig very bitter.

activities.title: Match the Cleaning Words
activities.prompt: Match each word with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Datun uses plant twigs. Reetha is one natural hair cleaner.

activities.title: Modern Brushing
activities.prompt: Where did the modern idea of brushing teeth come from?
options: An Indian hygiene tradition
A hair-cleaning tradition
A household-cleaning recipe
A plant-gathering method
activities.explanation: The modern idea came from an Indian hygiene tradition.

activities.title: Dadu's Cleaning Steps
activities.prompt: Put Dadu's steps in the correct order.
items: Get a fresh twig from nearby trees
Chew the twig to make a brush
Use it to clean your teeth
activities.explanation: Dadu gets a fresh twig, chews it, then uses it to clean his teeth.

activities.title: More Than Food Removal
activities.prompt: What can Dadu's twig do besides removing food particles?
options: Clean his hair naturally
Make a household recipe
Give his gums a massage
Bring a fresh twig
activities.explanation: The twig removes food particles and gives Dadu's gums a good massage.

activities.prompt: Dadu rubs a neem twig between his teeth. What does this show?
options: He is using datun to clean his teeth.
He is using datun to clean his hair.
He is using datun to clean his food.
He is using datun to clean his tongue.

This mistake mixes up tooth cleaning with hair cleaning.
This mistake treats food as the thing being cleaned.
This mistake treats the tongue as the main cleaning target.

activities.explanation: This is right because datun means using plant twigs to clean teeth.

activities.prompt: Food sticks between Dadu's teeth. What happens when he rubs the twig?
options: The food particles may come out.
The food particles may taste sweeter.
The food particles may become a brush.
The food particles may clean his gums.

This mistake confuses removing food with changing its taste.
This mistake reverses the twig's job as a brush.
This mistake reverses the roles of food and gums.

activities.explanation: This is right because the twig helps remove food stuck between teeth.

activities.prompt: Moyna wants to test both twigs fairly. What should she do?
options: Try both twigs the same way, then compare their taste.
Try only neem, because neem is very bitter.
Try only babool, because babool tastes better.
Ask Dadu, because he uses both kinds of twig.

why.Try only neem, because neem is very bitt: This mistake tests only one twig instead of comparing both.
why.Try only babool, because babool tastes b: This mistake checks one twig even though one taste is known.
why.Ask Dadu, because he uses both kinds of: This mistake asks Dadu instead of testing Moyna's own taste.

activities.explanation: This is right because the same way makes the taste comparison fair.

lessons.title: Home Cleaners and Animal Grooming

activities.prompt: How do homes and animals stay clean?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Keeping Homes and Animals Clean
activities.body: Cleaning agents remove dirt and germs from surfaces around our homes. We can make an eco-friendly cleaner with orange or lemon peels, spices, and white vinegar. Keep the mixture in a transparent container in a sunny place. After two weeks, strain the liquid. Animals also clean themselves. Monkeys groom each other, while birds use their beaks to clean feathers.
keyPoints: Cleaning agents remove dirt and germs.
We can make an eco-friendly cleaner at home.
Animals groom themselves in different ways.
activities.explanation: These ideas help us care for our homes and notice how animals stay clean.

activities.prompt: A monkey has insects on its fur. What should another monkey do?
steps: Monkeys groom each other because this keeps their bodies clean.
Grooming also helps keep their bodies free from insects.
So another monkey should groom it to help with the insects.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do cleaning agents remove from surfaces around our homes?
options: Dirt and germs
Peels and spices
Vinegar and water
Cups and buckets
activities.explanation: Cleaning agents remove dirt and germs from surfaces around our homes.

activities.prompt: We can make our own eco-friendly cleaner.
activities.explanation: Yes. We can make an eco-friendly cleaner with orange or lemon peels.

activities.prompt: We can add ______ cloves to our homemade cleaner.
activities.hint: Think of the number of cloves given in your book.
activities.explanation: Ten cloves can be added to the homemade cleaner.

activities.prompt: We keep the homemade cleaner in a dark place.
activities.explanation: Put the ingredients in a transparent container and keep it in a sunny place.

activities.prompt: Match each ingredient or container with its role.
pairs: Ten cloves or two or three bay leaves
activities.explanation: The peels, spices, and vinegar make the cleaner. The container is kept in a sunny place.

activities.prompt: Which benefit comes from monkey grooming?
options: Keep bodies clean and free from insects
Use beaks to clean their feathers
Make cleaner from peels and spices
Observe how insects clean themselves
activities.explanation: Monkeys groom each other to keep their bodies clean and free from insects. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: What can we do to learn about animal and insect cleaning?
options: Observe how they clean themselves
Give them orange peels
Cover them with vinegar
Strain their bodies
activities.explanation: We can observe how animals and insects clean themselves. This is a useful way to learn.

activities.prompt: The peels and spices are in a container. What should happen next?
options: White vinegar should cover them.
Sunlight should cover them.
Straining should cover them.
Bay leaves should cover them.

This mistakes the sunny place for an ingredient that covers things.
This mistakes a later step for the next ingredient step.
This mistakes an added spice for the liquid that covers the mixture.

activities.explanation: White vinegar covers the peels and spices.

activities.prompt: Today, the mixture is still in the sunny place. When should you strain the liquid?
options: After two weeks, when the all-purpose cleaner is ready.
Before adding vinegar, when the mixture is incomplete.
After adding more spices, when the mixture is just starting.
Before putting it in sunlight, when nothing has mixed.

why.Before adding vinegar, when the mixture: This mistakes an early ingredient step for the waiting time.
why.After adding more spices, when the mixtu: Adding spices is an early step, not the finishing time.
why.Before putting it in sunlight, when noth: Putting it in sunlight happens before the two-week wait.

activities.explanation: After two weeks, the strained liquid becomes the all-purpose cleaner.

lessons.title: Exercise for a Healthy Body

activities.prompt: What happens to our bodies when we play and move?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Exercise helps our body
activities.body: Exercise is good for the body. It can make us sweat and make our heart work harder. Fast running makes us breathe faster and deeper. You can also walk like a duck, jump like a frog, or run like a cat. With a skipping rope, you can count your jumps and invite a friend after ten jumps.
keyPoints: Exercise is good for the body.
Exercise can make us sweat.
Fast running makes us breathe faster and deeper.
activities.explanation: Exercise helps our body in many fun ways.

activities.prompt: After fast running, a child sweats and breathes faster and deeper. What is happening, and which exercise type fits?
steps: Fast running makes breathing faster and deeper, so the breathing change fits.
Exercise can make us sweat and make the heart work harder, so both body changes fit.
These changes show that the body is working hard during exercise.
Fast running fits the cardio-respiratory type because it makes breathing faster and deeper.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Three types of exercise
activities.body: Your body needs three main types of exercise. One type strengthens the cardio-respiratory system, which helps when you run fast. Another type adds strength to the muscles and bones. A third type maintains or improves flexibility. It helps your body bend and stretch. Different exercises can look like walking like a duck or jumping like a frog.
keyPoints: There are three main types of exercise.
One type strengthens the cardio-respiratory system.
Another type strengthens muscles and bones.
Another type maintains or improves flexibility.
activities.explanation: Different exercise types help our body in different ways.

activities.prompt: What can happen when we exercise?
options: You sweat and your heart works harder
You breathe slower and your heart rests
You stay cool and your heart stops
You sweat and your heart rests
activities.explanation: Exercise can make us sweat. It also makes our heart work harder.

activities.prompt: Fast running makes us breathe faster and ______.
activities.hint: Think about how you breathe when you run fast.
activities.explanation: Fast running makes us breathe faster and deeper.

activities.prompt: Exercise is good for the body.
activities.explanation: Yes! Exercise is good for the body. It helps us stay active and healthy.

activities.prompt: Which type of exercise maintains or improves flexibility?
options: It maintains or improves flexibility
It adds strength to muscles and bones
It strengthens the cardio-respiratory system
It makes the body sweat
activities.explanation: This type maintains or improves flexibility. The other types strengthen different parts of the body.

activities.prompt: Match each animal to the way we can move when we exercise.
activities.explanation: We can move like a duck, a frog, or a cat when we exercise.

activities.prompt: Put the skipping game steps in order.
activities.explanation: First, take the rope. Then skip ten times. After that, invite a friend to jump.

activities.prompt: A child skips ten times on a skipping rope. A friend is waiting nearby. What can happen next?
options: The child can invite the friend to jump.
The child can ask the friend to walk like a duck.
The child can ask the friend to jump like a frog.
The child can ask the friend to run like a cat.

why.The child can ask the friend to walk lik: This mistake thinks walking like a duck is the next step.
why.The child can ask the friend to jump lik: This mistake thinks jumping like a frog is the next step.
why.The child can ask the friend to run like: This mistake thinks running like a cat is the next step.

activities.explanation: This is right because a friend can be invited after ten jumps.

activities.prompt: The body needs three main types of exercise. Which activity gives the clearest sign of cardio-respiratory work?
options: Fast running with faster, deeper breathing.
Walking like a duck while exercising.
Jumping like a frog while exercising.
Skipping with a rope and counting jumps.

Walking like a duck is exercise, but no fact links it to breathing changes.
Jumping like a frog is exercise, but no fact links it to breathing changes.
Counting jumps is listed, but no fact links it to breathing changes.

activities.explanation: This is right because fast running makes breathing faster and deeper.

activities.prompt: A child wants stronger muscles and bones and better flexibility. Which pair of exercise types fits?
options: Add muscle and bone strength; maintain flexibility.
Strengthen cardio-respiratory system; maintain flexibility.
Add muscle and bone strength; only make us sweat.
Maintain flexibility; only strengthen breathing.

why.Strengthen cardio-respiratory system; ma: This mistake leaves out the type that adds muscle and bone strength.
why.Add muscle and bone strength; only make: This mistake mistakes sweating for the flexibility exercise type.
why.Maintain flexibility; only strengthen br: This mistake leaves out muscle and bone strength and misuses breathing.

activities.explanation: This is right because one type adds strength and another maintains flexibility.

activities.prompt: Exercise is good for the body. A child says it must always make us sweat. What is the best reply?
options: The lesson says exercise can make us sweat.
The lesson says exercise must always make us sweat.
The lesson says exercise can never make us sweat.
The lesson says exercise must never make us sweat.

why.The lesson says exercise must always mak: This mistake changes can into always.
why.The lesson says exercise can never make: This mistake changes can into never.
why.The lesson says exercise must never make: This mistake changes can into a rule against sweating.

activities.explanation: This is right because the fact says exercise can make us sweat.

lessons.title: Active Games and Playing Safely

activities.prompt: How can we have fun and stay safe while playing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Fun, Activity and Safety
activities.body: Keeping your body and mind active can be fun. She walks around the house and enjoys playing chess with Harpreet. Safety matters too, especially in public spaces where strangers may be present. Stay with a trusted adult. Politely refuse sweets from strangers. Refuse a ride from someone you do not know. Know the way home. Pay attention while playing. Parents may use a pre-decided password when sending a new person.
keyPoints: Keep both your mind and body active.
Stay with a trusted adult around strangers.
Know the way home and pay attention while playing.
activities.explanation: Active games and careful safety choices can help you have fun.

activities.prompt: You are in a public space with a trusted adult. A stranger offers you sweets. What should you do?
steps: Public spaces may contain strangers, so you need to stay careful.
You may interact because a trusted adult is with you.
You should refuse the sweets because the person is a stranger.
A polite refusal keeps you safe while having fun.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: We should not interact with strangers unless a ______ adult is with us.
activities.hint: Which kind of adult should be with you?
activities.explanation: A trusted adult should be with you. This helps you stay safe.

activities.prompt: Match each situation with the safe choice.
pairs: Someone you do not know offers a ride
A trusted adult is not with you
Parents may send a new person
activities.explanation: Each pair follows a safety rule from the lesson. These choices help you stay safe.

activities.prompt: We should politely accept sweets offered by a stranger.
activities.explanation: The lesson says to politely refuse sweets offered by a stranger.

activities.prompt: What should you do if a stranger offers you sweets?
options: Politely refuse them.
Accept them.
Eat them later.
Give them away.
activities.explanation: You should politely refuse sweets from a stranger. This keeps you safe while having fun.

activities.prompt: You are in a public space. Someone you do not know offers you a ride. What should you do?
options: Refuse the ride.
Accept the ride.
Ask for sweets.
Use a password.
activities.explanation: You should refuse a ride from someone you do not know. You should also know the way home.

activities.prompt: What may a parent use when sending a new person?
options: A pre-decided password
A public space
A chess game
An unknown rider
activities.explanation: Parents may use a pre-decided password when sending a new person.

activities.prompt: She plays chess and still walks a little. Which plan keeps her mind and body active?
options: Play chess, then walk around the house.
Play chess, then read one book.
Play chess, then sit beside a window.
Read one book, then watch a game.

This activates her mind but leaves her body sitting still.
This activates her mind but leaves her body sitting still.
Neither option makes her body active.

activities.explanation: Chess is a mind activity, and walking moves her body.

activities.prompt: You are in a public space without a trusted adult. A stranger asks to talk. What should you do?
options: Do not talk with them or go anywhere.
Keep talking to them until your adult arrives.
Take them home to play a friendly game.
Share your parent's pre-decided password with them.

why.Keep talking to them until your adult ar: This ignores the rule about strangers without a trusted adult.
This treats the stranger's request as safe without a trusted adult.
why.Share your parent's pre-decided password: This confuses a parent's password with permission to trust a stranger.

activities.explanation: Without a trusted adult, you should not interact with strangers.

activities.prompt: A trusted adult is with you in a public space. A stranger offers sweets. What should you do?
options: Refuse the sweets, but talk if needed.
Refuse both the talk and the sweets.
Take the sweets, but do not talk.
Leave without telling your trusted adult.

This ignores that a trusted adult makes interaction allowed.
This forgets that sweets from strangers should be refused.
why.Leave without telling your trusted adult: This treats every stranger as a reason to leave your adult.

activities.explanation: A trusted adult is present, but sweets from a stranger should be refused.

activities.prompt: Someone you do not know offers you a ride. You know the way home. Why should you refuse?
options: Knowing the way does not make an unknown person safe.
Knowing someone's name does not make that person trusted.
This thinks fun matters more than refusing unknown rides.
Knowing the way means you cannot refuse a ride.

why.Knowing someone's name does not make tha: Knowing someone's name does not make that person trusted.
why.This thinks fun matters more than refusi: This thinks fun matters more than refusing unknown rides.
why.Knowing the way means you cannot refuse: This mixes knowing the way with needing an unknown person's ride.

activities.explanation: Knowing the way home does not make someone we do not know safe.

lessons.title: Reflecting on a Healthy Week

activities.prompt: What could our feelings and habits tell us about our health?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Week of Health
activities.body: A weekly health table can track our habits for a week. Feelings such as sleepiness, hunger and tiredness can tell us something about our health. Good sleep, diet and exercise help us feel good. Choose an activity to do at least twice a week. Doing it regularly can improve our stamina.
keyPoints: A weekly health table tracks our habits.
Feelings can tell us something about our health.
Regular activity can improve our stamina.
activities.explanation: Tracking your week helps you notice habits and feelings.

activities.prompt: Moyna feels tired during the week and wants to reflect on her habits. What should she do?
steps: Make a weekly health table, because tracking habits makes them easier to see.
Record sleep, diet, exercise and feelings, because the table shows the week together.
Notice sleepiness, hunger and tiredness, because feelings can tell us about health.
Reflect on the table and choose an activity at least twice a week, because regular activity can improve stamina.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What can we make to track our habits?
options: A weekly health table
A monthly homework chart
A yearly weather chart
A daily game chart
activities.explanation: A weekly health table helps us track our habits.

activities.prompt: We should choose an activity to do at least ______ times a week.
activities.hint: The lesson says at least this many times each week.
activities.explanation: Choosing an activity at least twice a week helps you build a habit.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: Tell us something about our health
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an idea from this lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Show how you spent one whole day
activities.explanation: First divide the circle, then colour it to show your day.

activities.prompt: What can feelings such as sleepiness, hunger and tiredness tell us?
options: Something about our health
The weather outside
Our school timetable
Our age
activities.explanation: Feelings such as sleepiness, hunger and tiredness give us health information.

activities.prompt: Match Moyna's activities to the hours she spends.
activities.explanation: Moyna's example day shows eight hours sleeping, two eating and six studying.

activities.prompt: Feelings such as sleepiness, hunger and tiredness can tell us about health. What should the child do?
options: Notice the feeling and check what it shows.
Ignore it until the feeling disappears.
Feel the same way and change nothing.
Use it to stop all healthy habits.

This misses the body's signal that something may be amiss.
This ignores useful information about health.
This mistakes a body signal for a reason to stop helpful habits.

activities.explanation: Feelings can give useful information about health.

activities.prompt: Good sleep, diet and exercise help us feel good. Which plan is the fairest test of sleep and feelings?
options: Record sleep and feelings for one week.
Record sleep for one day only.
Record feelings before changing sleep.
Record sleep and feelings at different times.

One day does not follow the advice to track habits for a week.
This does not track the whole week of sleep and feelings.
why.Record sleep and feelings at different t: This makes the week's sleep and feelings hard to compare.

activities.explanation: This tracks both sleep and feelings throughout one week.

activities.prompt: We each need to know what is good for our body and mind. How can reflecting on a weekly table help?
options: It shows how habits and feelings go together.
It proves every feeling means the same thing.
It removes the need to notice tiredness.
It chooses healthy habits without any checking.

why.It proves every feeling means the same t: This mistakes different feelings for the same health message.
This wrongly treats the table as a reason to ignore body signals.
why.It chooses healthy habits without any ch: This imagines the table can choose instead of helping us notice.

activities.explanation: Tracking the week helps us notice which habits go with feeling good.

activities.prompt: Moyna sleeps for eight hours, eats for two, and studies for six. What should her circle show?
options: Sleep, eating and study in matching slices.
Only sleep in matching hour slices.
Only eating and study in matching slices.
Only studying in matching hour slices.

This leaves out eating and studying from Moyna's day.
why.Only eating and study in matching slices: This leaves out the eight hours Moyna spends sleeping.
This leaves out sleeping and eating from Moyna's day.

activities.explanation: Colouring matching slices shows how Moyna spends her day.

activities.prompt: Feelings can show what is amiss, and regular activity can improve stamina. Which plan should the child follow?
options: Track habits for a week, then repeat one activity.
Track feelings once, then stop watching habits.
Choose many activities, but never track habits.
Wait for feelings, and never do an activity.

why.Track feelings once, then stop watching: One check does not follow the advice to track habits for a week.
why.Choose many activities, but never track: This skips tracking and does not choose one regular activity.
why.Wait for feelings, and never do an activ: This ignores that regular activity can improve stamina.

activities.explanation: This combines a weekly table with regular activity that can improve stamina.

activities.context: Every morning, a student brushes their teeth, takes a shower, and combs their hair. After using the toilet and returning from outdoors, they wash their hands with soap. They rinse their mouth after eating and keep their nails trimmed and clean. During the day, the student repeats some washing habits because some daily activities are done more than once.
activities.prompt: The student has just used the toilet. What should they do next?
options: Use soap to clean their hands.
Rinse their mouth.
Comb their hair again.
Trim their nails again.

Rinsing the mouth is not the stated response here.
Combing the hair does not follow toilet use in the lesson.
Trimming the nails is not the stated response here.

activities.explanation: This is the required response after using the toilet.

activities.prompt: Why are clean daily habits important for our bodies?
activities.answer: Simple daily habits help keep our bodies clean. Good habits also help keep our bodies free from diseases. Brushing our teeth, showering, combing our hair, washing our hands with soap, and keeping our nails trimmed and clean are all important parts of a clean and healthy daily routine.
points: Daily habits keep the body clean.
Good habits help prevent diseases.
Several examples of clean habits are given.
The habits belong to a daily routine.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between datun and modern brushing.
activities.answer: Datun is a traditional way to clean teeth by using twigs of certain plants, such as neem, karanj and babool. Modern brushing is the newer idea, and it came from an Indian hygiene tradition. Thus, datun names the plant-twig method, while brushing teeth is the modern practice connected to that tradition.
points: Datun uses twigs of certain plants.
Neem, karanj and babool are examples.
The modern brushing idea came from an Indian hygiene tradition.
Datun is the traditional plant-twig method.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At home, a learner makes an eco-friendly cleaner. She puts the peels of eight oranges and ten cloves in a transparent container, then adds two cups of white vinegar to cover them. She leaves the container in a sunny place. She watches monkeys groom each other and a bird clean its feathers with its beak. She plans to mix one cup of the cleaner with a bucket of water for cleaning her home.
activities.prompt: The container has been left in a sunny place. What should the learner do next to finish the cleaner?
options: Strain the liquid after two weeks.
Strain the liquid immediately after adding the vinegar.
Use the liquid without straining it.
Wait in the sun until all the liquid has disappeared.

why.Strain the liquid immediately after addi: The vinegar and other ingredients must remain in the container for two weeks.
Straining is needed before the cleaner is ready.
why.Wait in the sun until all the liquid has: The instructions do not say to wait for the liquid to disappear.

activities.explanation: The recipe says to strain the liquid after two weeks.

activities.context: At home, a learner makes an eco-friendly cleaner. She puts the peels of eight oranges and ten cloves in a transparent container, then adds two cups of white vinegar to cover them. She leaves the container in a sunny place. She watches monkeys groom each other and a bird clean its feathers with its beak. She plans to mix one cup of the cleaner with a bucket of water for cleaning her home.
activities.prompt: If a monkey could no longer groom another monkey, what would be the likely result?
options: Its body might not stay clean and free from insects.
Its body would stay clean because insects would leave it.
Its body would need its beak to clean its feathers.
Its body would be cleaned by white vinegar.

why.Its body would stay clean because insect: This suggests that stopping grooming would cause insects to leave, which is not stated.
why.Its body would need its beak to clean it: This mixes up the monkey with the bird's beak-and-feathers action.
why.Its body would be cleaned by white vineg: White vinegar is an ingredient in the cleaner, not a method of monkey grooming.

activities.explanation: Grooming helps monkeys keep their bodies clean and free from insects.

activities.prompt: How does making our eco-friendly cleaner differ from the ways monkeys and birds clean themselves?
activities.answer: Our cleaner uses orange or lemon peels, cloves or bay leaves, and white vinegar. We keep the ingredients in a sunny place for two weeks, then strain the liquid. Monkeys groom each other to keep their bodies clean and free from insects. Birds use their beaks to clean their feathers.
points: The cleaner is made with fruit peels, spices, and white vinegar.
The ingredients are kept in the sun for two weeks before the liquid is strained.
Monkeys groom each other to keep their bodies clean and free from insects.
Birds use their beaks to clean their feathers.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child decides to exercise. First, the child runs fast for a while. The child’s breathing becomes faster and deeper, and exercise makes the child sweat while the heart works harder. Next, the child walks like a duck, jumps like a frog, and runs like a cat. Finally, the child takes a skipping rope and counts the jumps. After ten jumps, the child invites a friend to jump too.
activities.prompt: If the child keeps running fast, what is likely to happen next to the child’s breathing?
options: Take deeper breaths at a quicker rate.
Breathe more slowly and lightly than before.
Keep the same breathing speed and depth.
Breathe faster but with less depth each time.

why.Breathe more slowly and lightly than bef: Fast running does not slow the breathing.
Both the speed and depth of breathing change.
why.Breathe faster but with less depth each: The breathing becomes deeper, not less deep.

activities.explanation: This matches what happens during fast running.

activities.context: A child decides to exercise. First, the child runs fast for a while. The child’s breathing becomes faster and deeper, and exercise makes the child sweat while the heart works harder. Next, the child walks like a duck, jumps like a frog, and runs like a cat. Finally, the child takes a skipping rope and counts the jumps. After ten jumps, the child invites a friend to jump too.
activities.prompt: What should the child do after counting ten jumps with the skipping rope?
options: Invite a friend to join in the jumping.
Keep skipping by yourself instead of inviting anyone.
Invite the friend to watch without taking any jumps.
Wait until later before inviting a friend to jump.

why.Keep skipping by yourself instead of inv: This overlooks the invitation to a friend.
why.Invite the friend to watch without takin: The friend is invited to jump, not only watch.
why.Wait until later before inviting a frien: The invitation comes after the ten jumps.

activities.explanation: A friend is invited to jump after ten skips.

activities.prompt: How does fast running affect breathing?
activities.answer: Fast running causes breathing to become faster and deeper. The child will take breaths more often, and each breath will be deeper. This happens because the child is exercising, and exercise is good for the body.
points: Breathing becomes faster.
Breathing becomes deeper.
The change happens during exercise.
Exercise is good for the body.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: She still walks around the house a little and enjoys playing chess with Harpreet because she believes both her mind and body should be active. While she is in a public space, a stranger offers her sweets and asks for directions. Later, another person offers to drive her home. She knows the way home and remembers that staying safe matters while having fun. If a parent sends a new person, her parent will use a password they have decided beforehand.
activities.prompt: What should she do when the stranger offers her sweets?
options: She should refuse the sweets and leave without talking to the stranger.
She should accept the sweets because the stranger seems friendly.
She should accept the sweets if the stranger says they know her parents.
She should refuse the sweets but ask the stranger for directions.

why.She should accept the sweets because the: A friendly manner does not make a stranger safe.
why.She should accept the sweets if the stra: Knowing her parents does not remove the stranger risk.
why.She should refuse the sweets but ask the: Asking for directions would mean interacting without a trusted adult.

activities.explanation: Refusing protects her from accepting something from a stranger.

activities.context: She still walks around the house a little and enjoys playing chess with Harpreet because she believes both her mind and body should be active. While she is in a public space, a stranger offers her sweets and asks for directions. Later, another person offers to drive her home. She knows the way home and remembers that staying safe matters while having fun. If a parent sends a new person, her parent will use a password they have decided beforehand.
activities.prompt: If her parent sends a new person to collect her, what should she do before going with them?
options: She should ask for the password they decided beforehand.
She should go with them because her parent sent them.
She should let the new person choose any password.
She should go with them if they know her name.

why.She should go with them because her pare: Being sent by a parent does not mean she should skip the check.
why.She should let the new person choose any: A password should be decided beforehand, not chosen by the new person.
why.She should go with them if they know her: Knowing her name does not prove that she knows the person.

activities.explanation: The password helps her check the new person's message.

activities.context: Moyna makes a weekly health table. Each day, she records what she does and how she feels. On her example day, she colours a 24-slice circle: eight slices for sleeping, two for eating and six for studying. She notices when she feels sleepy or tired. After checking the table, she thinks about which habits are good for her body and mind.
activities.prompt: Moyna feels sleepy and tired. What should she do with her weekly health table?
options: Review her activities and feelings during the week.
Start a fresh table without using her feelings.
Record only the number of slices she colours.
Change her activities before checking how she felt.

why.Record only the number of slices she col: The number of coloured slices alone is incomplete.
why.Change her activities before checking ho: Changing activities first hides useful clues.

activities.explanation: Her feelings may point to a health need.

activities.context: Moyna makes a weekly health table. Each day, she records what she does and how she feels. On her example day, she colours a 24-slice circle: eight slices for sleeping, two for eating and six for studying. She notices when she feels sleepy or tired. After checking the table, she thinks about which habits are good for her body and mind.
activities.prompt: Why can Moyna's feelings be useful in her weekly health table?
options: They can show that something in her body or mind may need attention.
They can show that every activity she does is harmful.
They can show that she should always feel energetic.
They can show that feelings do not matter to health.

why.They can show that every activity she do: Some activities may be helpful, not harmful.
why.They can show that she should always fee: People can feel tired even when they are healthy.
why.They can show that feelings do not matte: Feelings are the body's way of sending messages.

activities.explanation: Feelings can give clues about health.

activities.prompt: Explain why we should track both our activities and our feelings in a weekly health table.
activities.answer: Tracking what we do and how we feel can show patterns across the week. Feelings such as sleepiness, hunger and tiredness can tell us that something is amiss. A weekly health table helps us notice these signals and learn what is good for our body and mind.
points: Activities and feelings are both tracked.
Sleepiness, hunger and tiredness give clues.
Feelings may show that something is amiss.
The table helps us learn what is good for us.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.title: A Daily Habit
activities.prompt: What should you do every day to keep your teeth clean?
options: Brush your teeth every day
Take a shower very rarely
Keep every nail long
Never wash your hands
activities.explanation: The lesson says we should brush our teeth every day. Good habits keep our bodies clean and free from diseases.

activities.prompt: We should wash our hands with soap after using the toilet.

activities.prompt: We should drink ______ glasses of water each day.
activities.hint: Choose the range given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The lesson tells us to drink 6–8 glasses of water each day.

activities.title: Make an Eco-Friendly Cleaner
activities.prompt: Put the steps for making the cleaner in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The liquid is ready after two weeks in sunshine. Straining it gives us our all-purpose cleaner.

activities.prompt: What does Dadu do to make his twig into a brush?
options: He chews the twig
He trims it with soap
He freezes it in water
He puts it in vinegar

activities.prompt: Only two main types of exercise are needed by the body.
activities.explanation: The body needs three main types of exercise. They help our body in different ways.

pairs: You are playing in a public space
activities.explanation: These choices help us stay safe while having fun in public spaces.

chapters.title: This World of Things
chapters.summary: In this chapter: metals and classroom materials; seeing through and using colours; materials around us; solids, liquids and gases.

lessons.title: Metals and Classroom Materials

activities.prompt: What metals are hiding in the things we use every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Metals and Other Materials
activities.body: Metals are taken out from inside Earth. Rock and sediment dug from inside Earth are called ore. Metals are carefully extracted from certain rock and sediment. Common metals include iron, copper, aluminium, gold, silver and mercury. An alloy is a mixture of metals. Steel, brass and bronze are alloys. Wood comes from trees. Glass is mostly made of sand. Clay and rubber are other materials found around us.
keyPoints: Metals come from rock and sediment inside Earth.
An alloy is a mixture of metals.
Wood, glass, clay and rubber are other materials.
activities.explanation: You can now tell metals, alloys and other materials apart.

activities.prompt: Khushi opens the door and asks where the metal in its hinges began.
steps: Khushi's hinges contain metals, so she follows where they began.
Metals are extracted from rock and sediment, so they begin inside Earth.
The dug rock and sediment is called ore, showing the source.
So the metal in Khushi's hinges was taken from inside Earth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Khushi's Furniture
activities.prompt: What are Khushi's table and chair made of?
options: Wood
Glass
Clay
Rubber
activities.explanation: Khushi's table and chair are made of wood. Wood comes from a tree.

activities.title: Glass and Clay
activities.prompt: Glass is mostly made of clay.
activities.explanation: Glass is mostly made of sand. Clay is another material found around us.

activities.title: Match Materials
activities.prompt: Match each material or object with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a material and what your book tells you about it.

activities.title: Find a Common Metal
activities.prompt: Which one is a common metal?
options: Iron
Clay
Rubber
Glass
activities.explanation: Iron is one of the common metals. Clay, rubber and glass are other materials.

activities.title: What Must an Alloy Be?
activities.prompt: A material is called an alloy. What must it be?
options: A mixture of metals
A type of ore
Mostly made of sand
Comes from a tree
activities.explanation: Alloys are mixtures of metals. Steel, brass and bronze are examples.

activities.title: Alloys and Metals
activities.prompt: Every alloy is a mixture of metals.
activities.explanation: An alloy is a mixture of metals. Steel, brass and bronze are examples.

activities.prompt: Imagine a new latch is made from copper. Where did its metal begin?
options: It began in rock and sediment inside Earth.
It began in a tree that became wood.
It began in sand that became glass.
It began in clay found around us.

This confuses a metal's source with wood's tree source.
This confuses a metal's source with glass's sand source.
This confuses a metal's source with clay being around us.

activities.explanation: This is right: copper comes from rock and sediment inside Earth.

activities.prompt: A child mixes copper and aluminium for a model. How should the child explain the result?
options: It is an alloy because the result mixes metals.
It is ore because the result came from inside Earth.
It is wood because one part came from a tree.
It is glass because one part is mostly sand.

why.It is ore because the result came from i: This confuses an alloy with ore, which is dug from Earth.
why.It is wood because one part came from a: This confuses a metal mixture with wood and its tree source.
why.It is glass because one part is mostly s: This confuses an alloy with glass, which is mostly made of sand.

activities.explanation: This is right because alloys are mixtures of metals.

activities.prompt: Rock and sediment are dug from inside Earth. A child calls the metal alone ore. Why is this wrong?
options: Ore is the dug rock and sediment, not only the metal.
Ore is the tree part left after wood is cut.
Ore is any mixture made from two metals.
Ore is sand after it has become glass.

why.Ore is the tree part left after wood is: This confuses ore with wood, which comes from a tree.
This confuses ore with an alloy, which mixes metals.
This confuses ore with glass, which is mostly made of sand.

activities.explanation: This is right because ore names rock and sediment dug from Earth.

activities.prompt: A child must sort wood pieces and metal pieces. Which check is fairest?
options: Check whether each begins at a tree or inside Earth.
Check whether each piece is common around us.
Check whether each piece is part of classroom furniture.
Check whether each piece is mostly made of sand.

why.Check whether each piece is common aroun: This confuses where a material begins with materials found around us.
why.Check whether each piece is part of clas: This confuses where a material begins with where an item is used.
why.Check whether each piece is mostly made: This confuses where a material begins with what glass is made from.

activities.explanation: This is right: wood comes from trees, but metals come from Earth.

activities.prompt: A child says steel, brass and bronze each contain only one metal. Why is this claim flawed?
options: They are alloys, so each one is a mixture of metals.
They are glasses, so each one is mostly made of sand.
They are ores, so each one was dug from inside Earth.
They are woods, so each one comes from a tree.

why.They are glasses, so each one is mostly: This confuses alloys with glass, which is mostly made of sand.
why.They are ores, so each one was dug from: This confuses alloys with ores dug from inside Earth.
why.They are woods, so each one comes from a: This confuses alloys with wood, which comes from a tree.

activities.explanation: This is right because steel, brass and bronze are alloy examples.

activities.prompt: Khushi's table comes from a tree. Which other material began inside Earth?
options: The nail, because metals are taken from inside Earth.
The chair, because wood also comes from trees.
The glass, because glass is mostly made of sand.
The clay, because clay is found around us.

why.The chair, because wood also comes from: This repeats the tree source already used by the table.
why.The glass, because glass is mostly made: This confuses metal's Earth source with glass being mostly made of sand.
why.The clay, because clay is found around u: This confuses being found around us with being taken from inside Earth.

activities.explanation: This is right because nails are metals taken from inside Earth.
