lessons.title: Seeing Through and Using Colours

activities.prompt: What helps us see through some materials but not others?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Looking Through Different Materials
activities.body: Khushi's windowpanes are made of glass. You can see flowers and trees through them. Glass is usually transparent, so you can see through it very clearly. A material seen through only partly is translucent. A material you cannot see through is opaque, like wood. See-through bags, bottles and thin cloth can have different colours.
keyPoints: Glass is usually transparent.
Translucent materials are seen through partly.
Opaque materials cannot be seen through.
activities.explanation: These words describe how clearly you can see through materials.

activities.prompt: Khushi wants to see flowers through her window. Should the pane be glass or wood?
steps: Glass is transparent because you can see through it.
Wood is opaque because you cannot see through it.
Glass fits because Khushi needs to see the flowers.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What are Khushi's windowpanes made of?
options: Glass
Wood
Flowers
Trees
activities.explanation: Khushi's windowpanes are made of glass.

activities.prompt: A material that you can see through is called ______.
activities.hint: Think about what you can see through.
activities.explanation: A transparent material lets you see through it.

activities.prompt: Which material is opaque?
options: Glass
Wood
Thin cloth
Bags
activities.explanation: Wood is opaque, so you cannot see through it.

activities.prompt: What is a material called when you can see through it only partly?
options: Opaque
Transparent
Translucent
Glass
activities.explanation: A translucent material can be seen through only partly.

activities.prompt: Match each way of seeing to its material word.
activities.explanation: Transparent means see-through, translucent means partly see-through, and opaque means not see-through.

activities.prompt: Which pair of materials is correct?
options: Glass is transparent; wood is opaque.
Glass is opaque; wood is transparent.
Glass is translucent; wood is transparent.
Glass is transparent; wood is translucent.
activities.explanation: Glass is transparent, but wood is opaque.

activities.prompt: A wooden board covers a flower. What can Khushi see through the board?
options: She will see the flowers clearly.
She will see the flowers partly.
She will not see the flowers.
She will see the board's colour.

This wrongly treats wood as transparent.
This wrongly treats wood as translucent.
Seeing the board's colour is not seeing through the board.

activities.explanation: Wood is opaque, so Khushi cannot see through it.

activities.prompt: You have a wooden board. How can you test whether it is opaque?
options: Check whether the board has changed colour.
Try to see an object through the board.
Touch the board and feel its surface.
Hold the board against a glass pane.

why.Check whether the board has changed colo: Looking at colour does not test whether you can see through it.
Feeling the board does not test whether you can see through it.
Holding it against glass does not test the board itself.

activities.explanation: Looking through the board checks whether you can see through it.

activities.prompt: A child says wood is transparent. The child gives glass as the reason. What is wrong?
options: Glass is opaque, so wood must be transparent.
Glass and wood must both be transparent.
Wood is opaque, unlike transparent glass.
Wood is translucent, so the child is partly right.

why.Glass is opaque, so wood must be transpa: This swaps the facts about glass and wood.
The claim wrongly treats glass and wood as the same.
why.Wood is translucent, so the child is par: Wood is opaque, so it is not partly see-through.

activities.explanation: Glass is transparent, but wood is opaque, so the reason fails.

activities.prompt: A transparent sheet and a translucent sheet cover a flower. What can you see through them?
options: You will see the flower clearly through both sheets.
You will see one partly and not see the other.
You will see the flower through neither sheet.
You will see one clearly and the other partly.

why.You will see the flower clearly through: This wrongly treats the translucent sheet as transparent.
why.You will see one partly and not see the: This wrongly treats the translucent sheet as opaque.
why.You will see the flower through neither: This wrongly treats the transparent sheet as opaque.

activities.explanation: The transparent sheet is clear, while the translucent sheet shows only partly.

activities.prompt: A bag and a bottle have different colours. What can both materials be?
options: Both must be opaque.
Both must be translucent.
Both can be transparent.
Neither can be transparent.

Different colours do not make these see-through materials opaque.
This confuses transparent materials with partly see-through materials.
This wrongly says different colours stop transparency.

activities.explanation: See-through bags and bottles can have different colours.

lessons.title: Materials Around Us

activities.prompt: What clues can help us discover the materials in things around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Different Materials
activities.body: Wood is hard and rigid. Khushi's table is made of wood. Fabric is soft and flexible. Flexible fabric is suitable for making clothes and curtains. Different materials may look different. Words like smooth, rough, cold to touch, dull and shiny describe them. Tap a metal spoon on different objects to compare their sounds. Describe sounds with short words such as ting-ting, then compose your own beats from the sounds.
keyPoints: Wood is hard and rigid.
Fabric is soft and flexible.
Tapping different objects lets you compare sounds.
activities.explanation: You can describe materials by their qualities, looks and sounds.

activities.prompt: Khushi wants to make a curtain. Should she use wood or fabric?
steps: Wood is not the best choice because it is hard and rigid.
Fabric is a better choice because it is soft and flexible.
Curtains need flexible fabric because it is suitable for making them.
Therefore, Khushi should choose fabric for the curtain.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Khushi's Table
activities.prompt: What is Khushi's table made of?
options: wood
fabric
metal
activities.explanation: Khushi's table is made of wood. Wood is hard and rigid.

activities.title: Making with Fabric
activities.prompt: Flexible fabric is suitable for making ______ and curtains.
activities.hint: It is listed beside curtains.
activities.explanation: Flexible fabric is suitable for making clothes and curtains.

activities.title: Material Matches
activities.prompt: Match each item with the right material or description.
activities.explanation: Khushi's table is wooden. The spoon is metal. Flexible fabric suits clothes and curtains.

activities.title: Compare Sounds
activities.prompt: What can tapping a metal spoon on different objects let you compare?
options: their sounds
their smoothness
their roughness
their shininess
activities.explanation: Tapping a metal spoon on different materials lets you compare their sounds.

activities.title: Choose the Right Things
activities.prompt: Which things can flexible fabric be suitable for making?
options: clothes and curtains
wood and metal
hardness and rigidity
softness and flexibility
activities.explanation: Flexible fabric is suitable for making clothes and curtains.

activities.title: Make Your Own Beats
activities.prompt: Put the steps for making your own beats in order.
items: Tap a metal spoon on different objects.
activities.explanation: First compare the sounds. Then describe them and use them to compose beats.

activities.prompt: Khushi's table is made of wood. Wood is hard and rigid. Which item would be difficult to fold?
options: The wooden table, because wood is hard and rigid.
The wooden table, because fabric is soft and flexible.
The fabric, because fabric is soft and flexible.
The fabric, because wood is hard and rigid.

why.The wooden table, because fabric is soft: This mixes the table's wood with fabric's soft, flexible qualities.
why.The fabric, because fabric is soft and f: Fabric is soft and flexible, so it would be easier to fold.
why.The fabric, because wood is hard and rig: This applies wood's hard, rigid qualities to the fabric.

activities.explanation: Wood is hard and rigid, so the table would be difficult to fold.

activities.prompt: Khushi's table is made of wood. Her curtain is made of fabric. What may happen when you look at them?
options: They may look different because their materials are different.
They must look different because their materials are different.
They may look the same because their materials are different.
They must look the same because their materials are different.

why.They must look different because their m: It changes a possible difference into a certainty.
why.They may look the same because their mat: It claims sameness, while the fact gives a possible difference.
why.They must look the same because their ma: It changes a possible difference into both certainty and sameness.

activities.explanation: The fact says different materials may look different.

activities.prompt: You plan to tap a wooden table and some fabric. You want a fair sound test. What should you do?
options: Tap both with the same metal spoon.
Look at both with the same metal spoon.
Touch both with the same metal spoon.
Hold both near the same metal spoon.

Looking at the spoon does not compare tapping sounds.
Touching with the spoon is not the given tapping test.
Holding objects near it does not compare their tapping sounds.

activities.explanation: Tapping both with one metal spoon compares their different sounds.

activities.prompt: Different materials may look different. Tapping a metal spoon compares sounds. This test shows how every material looks. What is wrong with this claim?
options: It compares sounds, not how materials look.
It compares looks, not how materials sound.
It proves that all materials look the same.
It finds the exact word for each sound.

why.It compares looks, not how materials sou: This mistake swaps what tapping compares with what looking shows.
why.It proves that all materials look the sa: The claim is about showing looks, not proving sameness.
Naming sounds does not test how materials look.

activities.explanation: Tapping compares sounds, while the claim says it shows looks.

lessons.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases

activities.prompt: Why do some things keep their shape while others flow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three groups of matter
activities.body: A solid keeps its shape. Stones, bricks and wood are solid materials. A liquid flows and does not keep its shape. Water is a liquid. It stays in a cup when poured into it. Air is a gas. It floats in and out instead of staying in a cup. Objects can be classified as solids, liquids and gases. Sand, sponge and clay can be difficult to classify.
keyPoints: A solid does not change its shape.
Water is a liquid because it flows.
Air is a gas that floats in and out.
activities.explanation: Solids keep their shape, while liquids and gases flow.

activities.prompt: Why does water stay in a cup while air does not?
steps: Water flows because it is a liquid without a fixed shape.
When water is poured into a cup, it stays there.
The cup holds the water, so the water has the cup's shape.
Air floats in and out instead, because it is a gas.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sorting objects
activities.body: Objects can be classified as solids, liquids and gases. A solid does not change its shape. Water is a liquid because it flows. Air is a gas, and it flows differently from water. Some things are hard to place in a group. Sand, sponge and clay can be difficult to classify.
keyPoints: Objects belong to groups called solids, liquids and gases.
Solids keep their shape.
Some materials are difficult to classify.
activities.explanation: Classification means sorting objects into groups.

activities.title: Which one keeps its shape?
activities.prompt: Which one keeps its own shape without changing?
options: Stone
Water
Air
Sand
activities.explanation: Stone is a solid material. A solid does not change its shape.

activities.title: Water in a cup
activities.prompt: Water stays in a cup when it is poured into it.
activities.explanation: Yes! Water stays in a cup when it is poured into it.

activities.title: The flowing group
activities.prompt: Water is a ______. It flows, so it does not keep its shape.
activities.hint: What is water called when it flows?
activities.explanation: Water is a liquid. Liquids flow and do not keep their shape.

activities.title: Match each thing
activities.prompt: Match each thing to its group.
activities.explanation: Bricks are solid, water is liquid, and air is a gas.

activities.title: Pouring water
activities.prompt: What happens when water is poured into a cup?
options: It stays inside the cup.
It floats in and out.
It keeps its own shape.
It changes into air.
activities.explanation: Water stays inside the cup. Air floats in and out instead.

activities.title: Difficult to classify
activities.prompt: Which group is called difficult to classify?
options: Sand, sponge and clay
Sand, sponge and wood
Air, sponge and clay
Brick, sponge and clay
activities.explanation: Sand, sponge and clay are called difficult to classify.

activities.prompt: You pour water into one cup. You leave air near another cup. What happens?
options: Water stays in the cup.
Air stays in the cup.
Water stays, but air moves away.
Both water and air stay.

Water stays because that is what water does when poured.
This mistake treats air like water, but air moves in and out.
This mistake ignores that air does not stay in a cup.

activities.explanation: Water stays in the cup, while air floats in and out.

activities.prompt: Water flows around your hand. What does this show about water?
options: It is a solid with a fixed shape.
It is a liquid without a fixed shape.
It is a gas that floats away.
It is hard to classify, like clay.

This mistake thinks flowing water keeps a fixed shape like a solid.
This mistake confuses water with air, the gas that floats.
This mistake confuses water with clay, which can be hard to classify.

activities.explanation: Water flows because it is a liquid without a fixed shape.

activities.prompt: A child says water is solid because it has a cup's shape. What is wrong?
options: Water is solid because the cup is solid.
Water is liquid because it flows.
Water is gas because it floats.
Water is hard to classify, like clay.

This mistake uses the cup's shape instead of water's own shape.
This mistake confuses water with air, which floats in and out.
This mistake confuses a known liquid with a material that is hard to classify.

activities.explanation: Water flows and does not keep its own shape, so it is a liquid.

activities.prompt: Air and water both flow near a cup. What do you predict?
options: Both will stay inside the cup.
Water will stay, but air will move.
Air will stay, but water will move.
Both will flow away from the cup.

This mistake treats air like water, but air does not stay.
Air moves, while water stays, so this swaps their behaviour.
This mistake ignores that water stays in a cup.

activities.explanation: Water stays when poured, while air flows in and out.

activities.prompt: You have sand, a sponge, and clay. How can you test how to classify them?
options: Watch how each keeps or changes its shape.
Pour water into each and watch it flow.
Put air near each and watch it float.
Test only whether each can make a wall.

This mistake adds water instead of testing each material alone.
This mistake uses moving air instead of the material's own shape.
This mistake tests wall use instead of solid, liquid, or gas.

activities.explanation: A solid keeps its shape, so each material's shape is the useful clue.

lessons.title: Natural and Artificial Things

activities.prompt: How can we tell if something is natural or made by people?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Natural and Artificial Things
activities.body: Natural things exist without people making them. Some are alive, like plants and animals. Others are not alive, like rocks, water and air. Artificial things are made by people. Clothes, shoes and tables are examples. People can also make similar materials artificially. Very similar wax can be made from petroleum. Petroleum is found deep underground. Waste from petroleum-based materials does not biodegrade. This means it does not break down naturally.
keyPoints: Natural things may be living or non-living.
Artificial things are made by people.
Some artificial materials create waste that does not biodegrade.
activities.explanation: You have learned how people make artificial things from different materials.

activities.prompt: A child holds a mango and wax made from petroleum. How can the child sort them?
steps: The mango is natural because people did not make it.
The wax is artificial because people make it from petroleum.
Artificial materials can look similar, so appearance does not decide the group.
So the mango belongs with natural things, and the wax belongs with artificial things.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which one is a non-living natural thing?
options: Mango
Bird
Rock
Shoe
activities.explanation: Rocks are non-living natural things. Shoes are artificial things.

activities.prompt: Clothes, shoes and ______ are artificial things.
activities.hint: It is something people make.
activities.explanation: Tables are artificial things, like clothes and shoes.

activities.prompt: What happens to waste from petroleum-based materials?
options: It breaks down naturally.
It does not biodegrade.
It becomes living matter.
It becomes part of plants.
activities.explanation: Petroleum-based materials create waste that does not biodegrade.

activities.prompt: Which statement about artificial wax is true?
options: It is a natural thing.
It comes from petroleum.
It biodegrades quickly.
It lives deep underground.
activities.explanation: Very similar wax can be made from petroleum.

activities.prompt: Which group contains only artificial things?
options: Tree and bird
Mango and air
Clothes and shoes
Rock and water
activities.explanation: Clothes and shoes are artificial because people make them.

activities.prompt: A child throws away wax made from petroleum. What will happen to the waste?
options: The waste will biodegrade slowly.
The waste will not biodegrade.
The waste will become a natural liquid.
The waste will grow into a plant.

This wrongly assumes petroleum-based waste can break down naturally.
This confuses non-biodegradable waste with a natural material.
This wrongly treats non-biodegradable waste as living natural matter.

activities.explanation: Petroleum-based materials create waste that does not biodegrade.

activities.prompt: A bird flies over a rock. Both come from nature. What difference matters?
options: The bird is alive; the rock is not.
The rock is alive; the bird is not.
Both are alive because both can move.
Both are not alive because both stay still.

This wrongly reverses which thing is alive.
Moving does not decide whether something is living.
why.Both are not alive because both stay sti: This wrongly treats stillness as proof of being non-living.

activities.explanation: Plants and animals are living natural things, but rocks are non-living.

activities.prompt: A teacher says clothes are natural because people wear them. Why is this claim flawed?
options: Clothes are made by people, so they are artificial.
Clothes stay natural because people wear them.
Natural things are made by people every day.
Clothes stop being artificial once people wear them.

why.Clothes stay natural because people wear: This wrongly thinks wearing makes something natural.
why.Natural things are made by people every: This reverses what natural and artificial mean.
why.Clothes stop being artificial once peopl: This wrongly thinks wearing removes artificial status.

activities.explanation: Things made by people are artificial, and clothes are artificial things.

activities.prompt: A child sorts a mango, bird, table, and shoes. Which test separates natural and artificial things?
options: Check whether people made each thing.
Check whether each thing can move.
Check whether each thing can be picked.
Check whether each thing can be used.

Moving does not decide whether something is natural or artificial.
A mango can be picked but remains natural.
A table can be used but remains artificial.

activities.explanation: Natural things are not made by people, while artificial things are.

lessons.sceneAlt: Six round samples show beryllium copper, Inconel, steel, titanium, aluminium and magnesium.

activities.context: Khushi helps tidy the classroom after a lesson. She notices that the table and chair are made of wood, while the door has metal hinges, nails and latches. Her teacher says those metals came through extraction from inside Earth, where certain rock and sediment had been dug out as ore. The teacher points out that the brass hinge combines metals, while a glass item is mostly made of sand, and reminds the class that wood comes from a tree.
activities.prompt: Why can the metal latch be linked to the lesson about obtaining metals?
options: Obtaining its metal involved extraction from within Earth.
Its metal was obtained from a tree.
Its metal was made by mixing glass with sand.
Its metal was carefully extracted from clay or rubber.

Wrong: a tree is the source of wood.
why.Its metal was made by mixing glass with: Wrong: sand is mainly used to make glass.
why.Its metal was carefully extracted from c: Wrong: clay and rubber are other classroom materials, not the stated metal source.

activities.explanation: Correct: metals are taken out from inside Earth.

activities.context: Khushi helps tidy the classroom after a lesson. She notices that the table and chair are made of wood, while the door has metal hinges, nails and latches. Her teacher says those metals came through extraction from inside Earth, where certain rock and sediment had been dug out as ore. The teacher points out that the brass hinge combines metals, while a glass item is mostly made of sand, and reminds the class that wood comes from a tree.
activities.prompt: If Khushi replaced the metal latch with a wooden one, which statement would best explain the new latch?
options: Its material would still be taken out from inside Earth.
It would use material sourced from a tree.
Its material would be a mixture of metals.
Its material would be mostly made of sand.

why.Its material would still be taken out fr: Wrong: extraction from inside Earth is connected with metals.
why.Its material would be a mixture of metal: Wrong: a mixture of metals is an alloy.
why.Its material would be mostly made of san: Wrong: material mostly made of sand is glass.

activities.explanation: Correct: wood comes from a tree.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a common metal and an alloy.
activities.answer: Common metals include iron, copper, aluminium, gold, silver and mercury. Steel, brass and bronze are different because they are alloys. An alloy is a mixture of metals, so it contains more than one metal together.
points: Names common metals.
Identifies steel, brass and bronze as alloys.
Explains that an alloy is a mixture of metals.
Explains that an alloy contains more than one metal.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Khushi looks through the glass windowpanes of her home. She touches one pane with her hand and can still see the flowers and trees outside through the glass. Later, she looks through a coloured see-through bag and a thin cloth. The flowers can be seen through the cloth only partly. Khushi wonders what she would see if the windowpanes were made of wood instead of glass.
activities.prompt: If Khushi's windowpanes were made of wood instead of glass, what would happen?
options: She would not see the flowers and trees through the windowpanes.
She would see the flowers and trees very clearly through the wood.
She would see the flowers and trees only partly through the wood.
She would see only the colours of the flowers and trees through the wood.

why.She would see the flowers and trees very: This wrongly treats wood as transparent.
why.She would see the flowers and trees only: This wrongly treats wood as translucent.
why.She would see only the colours of the fl: This wrongly suggests that only colours can pass through wood.

activities.explanation: Wood is opaque, so she cannot see through it.

activities.context: Khushi looks through the glass windowpanes of her home. She touches one pane with her hand and can still see the flowers and trees outside through the glass. Later, she looks through a coloured see-through bag and a thin cloth. The flowers can be seen through the cloth only partly. Khushi wonders what she would see if the windowpanes were made of wood instead of glass.
activities.prompt: What is the bag like if Khushi can see through it?
options: The bag is opaque because it has a colour.
The bag is translucent because its colour changes what she sees.
The bag is transparent.
The bag must be made of glass.

why.The bag is opaque because it has a colou: A coloured material can still be transparent.
why.The bag is translucent because its colou: Being translucent means being seen through only partly.
See-through bags can have different colours and need not be glass.

activities.explanation: A material that can be seen through is called transparent.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between transparent, translucent and opaque materials.
activities.answer: A transparent material can be seen through clearly. A translucent material can be seen through only partly. An opaque material cannot be seen through at all. Glass is transparent, wood is opaque, and a thin cloth may be translucent if objects can be seen through it only partly.
points: Transparent means it can be seen through.
Translucent means it can be seen through only partly.
Opaque means it cannot be seen through.
Glass and wood are given as examples.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Khushi has a wooden table that is hard and rigid. She is making a curtain and needs a soft, flexible material. She also has a metal spoon and objects made from different materials. Khushi taps the spoon on them to explore the sounds. She describes some sounds with short words and can also make her own beats from the sounds she hears.
activities.prompt: Which reason best explains why fabric should be chosen for the curtain?
options: Flexible fabric is suitable for making curtains and clothes.
Wood is hard and rigid, so it should be suitable for a curtain.
Tapping different objects can produce sounds for making beats.
Different materials may look different, so appearance is the main reason for choosing fabric.

why.Wood is hard and rigid, so it should be: Hard and rigid wood is not identified as suitable for curtains.
why.Tapping different objects can produce so: Making beats is connected with sounds, not choosing curtain material.
why.Different materials may look different,: Looking different does not explain why fabric suits a curtain.

activities.explanation: This gives the correct property and use.

activities.context: Khushi has a wooden table that is hard and rigid. She is making a curtain and needs a soft, flexible material. She also has a metal spoon and objects made from different materials. Khushi taps the spoon on them to explore the sounds. She describes some sounds with short words and can also make her own beats from the sounds she hears.
activities.prompt: What should Khushi do next to compare the sounds of different materials?
options: Tap the metal spoon on objects made from different materials.
Tap the metal spoon only on the wooden table.
Use appearance alone instead of tapping the objects.
Make beats from one object's sound instead of testing different materials.

why.Tap the metal spoon only on the wooden t: One object does not allow a comparison between materials.
why.Use appearance alone instead of tapping: Appearance cannot show how the materials sound.
why.Make beats from one object's sound inste: Making beats is not the same as comparing different sounds.

activities.explanation: Tapping different materials allows their sounds to be compared.

activities.prompt: Explain why Khushi's table can stay firm.
activities.answer: Khushi's table is made of wood, and wood is hard and rigid. These properties explain why it can stay firm. A soft, flexible material would not have the same firm qualities as the wood used for her table.
points: The table is made of wood.
Wood is hard.
Wood is rigid.
Hard and rigid properties explain firmness.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child builds a wall with stones and bricks and places a cup beside it. The child pours water into the cup, where it stays. Later, the child opens a window, and air flows in and out of the room. The child also looks at sand, a sponge and clay and wonders whether each is a solid, a liquid or a gas.
activities.prompt: If the child pours the water from the cup into another cup, what should happen next?
options: The water will flow into the other cup and remain there.
The water will keep the shape of the first cup.
The air will float in and out of the other cup.
The water will keep one fixed shape and will not flow.

why.The water will keep the shape of the fir: This mistake treats water like a solid.
why.The air will float in and out of the oth: This mistake mixes up water and air.
why.The water will keep one fixed shape and: This mistake also treats water like a solid.

activities.explanation: Correct: water flows and stays in a cup.

activities.context: A child builds a wall with stones and bricks and places a cup beside it. The child pours water into the cup, where it stays. Later, the child opens a window, and air flows in and out of the room. The child also looks at sand, a sponge and clay and wonders whether each is a solid, a liquid or a gas.
activities.prompt: If the child tried to replace the stones and bricks in the wall with water, what would happen?
options: The water would flow away instead of holding the shape of the wall.
The water would keep the wall's shape because it is being used to build it.
The water would float in and out of the wall like air.
The water would be easy to classify as a solid because walls use solid materials.

why.The water would keep the wall's shape be: This mistake treats water like a solid material.
why.The water would float in and out of the: This mistake mixes up water and air.
why.The water would be easy to classify as a: This mistake confuses a liquid with a solid.

activities.explanation: Correct: water flows and does not keep its shape.

activities.prompt: Explain why solid materials are suitable for making walls.
activities.answer: Solids do not change their shape. Stones, bricks and wood are solid materials used to make walls. This means a wall made from solid materials can keep its shape. Water is different because it is a liquid: it flows and does not keep its shape.
points: Solids do not change their shape.
Stones, bricks and wood are used to make walls.
Solid materials can keep the shape of a wall.
Water flows and does not keep its shape.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child is helping with a craft project and needs wax. The child finds wax that was made from petroleum and learns that very similar wax can be made artificially from petroleum. Petroleum is a liquid found deep underground. The wax is artificial because people made it. The child sees a tree outside. It was not made by people, so it is natural. After the project, the child wonders what will happen to any waste from the petroleum-based wax.
activities.prompt: What will happen to any waste left from the petroleum-based wax?
options: It will remain without biodegrading.
It will biodegrade.
It will biodegrade after it is buried.
It will biodegrade after people use it.

This mistake assumes that all materials biodegrade.
Being buried does not make petroleum-based waste biodegrade.
People using the wax does not make its waste biodegrade.

activities.explanation: Petroleum-based materials create waste that does not biodegrade.

activities.context: A child is helping with a craft project and needs wax. The child finds wax that was made from petroleum and learns that very similar wax can be made artificially from petroleum. Petroleum is a liquid found deep underground. The wax is artificial because people made it. The child sees a tree outside. It was not made by people, so it is natural. After the project, the child wonders what will happen to any waste from the petroleum-based wax.
activities.prompt: If the child wants to avoid creating petroleum-based waste, what should the child do?
options: Use a different material that is not petroleum-based.
Use petroleum-based wax because petroleum is found underground.
Use petroleum-based wax because similar wax can be made artificially.
Use petroleum-based wax because petroleum is a liquid.

why.Use petroleum-based wax because petroleu: Finding petroleum underground does not prevent petroleum-based waste from failing to biodegrade.
why.Use petroleum-based wax because similar: Making similar wax artificially still creates the waste problem described in the case.
why.Use petroleum-based wax because petroleu: Petroleum being liquid does not change what happens to petroleum-based waste.

activities.explanation: A material that is not petroleum-based will not create the waste described in the case.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between natural things and artificial things using the case.
activities.answer: Natural things exist naturally and may be alive or not alive. The tree is a living natural thing because plants are living natural things. The petroleum-based wax is artificial because people made it. Being similar to another material does not make the wax natural.
points: Natural things exist naturally.
Natural things may be alive or not alive.
The tree is a living natural thing.
Things made by people are artificial.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.title: Khushi's Table
activities.prompt: What is Khushi's table made of?
options: glass
wood
clay
rubber
activities.explanation: Khushi's table and chair are made of wood. Great spotting!

activities.prompt: Match each material with its property or state.
activities.explanation: Wood is rigid, fabric is flexible, and glass is transparent. Water is liquid. Air is gas.

activities.prompt: Which group contains only examples of alloys?
options: Iron, copper and aluminium
Steel, brass and bronze
Glass, sand and clay
Wood, clay and rubber
activities.explanation: Steel, brass and bronze are examples of alloys. Alloys are mixtures of metals.

activities.prompt: An opaque material lets you see clearly through it.
activities.explanation: Opaque means you cannot see through a material. Transparent materials can be seen through very clearly.

activities.prompt: Petroleum-based materials create waste that does not ______.
activities.hint: The lesson gives the full phrase 'does not biodegrade'.
activities.explanation: Petroleum-based materials create waste that does not biodegrade.

activities.prompt: Order these materials from most see-through to least see-through.
activities.explanation: Transparent lets you see clearly. Translucent lets you see partly. Opaque cannot be seen through.

activities.prompt: Which set contains only artificial things?
options: Clothes, shoes and tables
Plants and animals
Rocks, water and air
A tree, a mango and a bird
activities.explanation: Clothes, shoes and tables are artificial things. People make them.

activities.prompt: Tapping a metal spoon on different materials helps compare their sounds.
activities.explanation: Different materials make sounds you can compare. You can even compose your own beats.

chapters.title: Making Things
chapters.summary: In this chapter: clay becomes a pot; patterns and ideas; bricks and buildings; mud houses.

lessons.title: Clay Becomes a Pot

activities.prompt: How does soft clay become a pot?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How a Pot Is Made
activities.body: Appooppan is Mini’s grandfather, and he makes pots. He wets the clay and adds water until it is just right. It must be neither too watery nor too dry. He pounds and kneads the clay like dough. He shapes it on a spinning stone wheel. Ammu moves dried pots into the potter’s oven, called a kiln. Fire bakes the pots. Later, the family makes patterns on some pots.
keyPoints: The clay must be just right for shaping.
Appooppan shapes the clay on a stone wheel.
Fire in the kiln bakes the pots.
activities.explanation: This shows you how careful clay preparation helps Appooppan make pots.

activities.prompt: Why must Appooppan check the clay before shaping a pot?
steps: He adds water until the clay is just right for shaping.
This matters because clay must be neither too watery nor too dry.
He pounds and kneads the clay well, like dough, before shaping it.
He spins the clay on a stone wheel to shape it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Kiln and the Patterns
activities.body: Appooppan shapes the clay by spinning it on a stone wheel. After the pots have dried, Ammu moves them into the potter’s oven. This oven is called a kiln. The fire inside the kiln bakes the pots. The family also makes patterns on some pots.
keyPoints: A kiln is the potter’s oven.
Fire inside the kiln bakes the pots.
The family makes patterns on some pots.
activities.explanation: You now know the special jobs of the kiln, the fire, and the family.

activities.prompt: What does Appooppan make?
options: Wet clay
Pots
Patterns
Water
activities.explanation: Appooppan is Mini’s grandfather, and he makes pots.

activities.prompt: The clay must be neither too watery nor too ______.
activities.hint: Think about the two kinds of clay that cannot be shaped well.
activities.explanation: Good! The clay needs the right amount of water for shaping.

activities.prompt: Match each person or thing with the correct job.
activities.explanation: You matched each action with the right part of the pot-making story.

activities.prompt: Why does Appooppan add water to the clay?
options: The clay becomes too watery for shaping.
The clay becomes too dry for shaping.
The clay becomes just right for shaping.
The clay becomes hard to shape.
activities.explanation: He adds water until the clay is just right, neither too watery nor too dry.

activities.prompt: Put the pot-making steps in order.
items: He pounds and kneads the clay.
He shapes it on a stone wheel.
Ammu moves the dried pots into the kiln.
activities.explanation: You followed the clay from wet clay to a baked pot.

activities.prompt: Which story matches the lesson?
options: Ammu shapes the clay before Mini moves the dried pots into the kiln.
Mini shapes the clay before Ammu moves the dried pots into the kiln.
The family shapes the clay before Mini moves the dried pots into the oven.
Appooppan shapes the clay before Ammu moves the dried pots into the kiln.
activities.explanation: Appooppan shapes the clay, and Ammu moves the dried pots into the kiln. You followed both parts correctly.

activities.prompt: Appooppan's clay is too dry for shaping. He has water. What should he do next, and why?
options: Add water until the clay is neither too watery nor too dry.
Add water until the clay is always as watery as possible.
Shape it now, because clay can also be shaped when dry.
Leave it alone, because clay should always be as dry as possible.

why.Add water until the clay is always as wa: This mistakes very watery clay for clay that is ready.
why.Shape it now, because clay can also be s: This forgets that clay must not be too dry for shaping.
why.Leave it alone, because clay should alwa: This mistakes very dry clay for clay that is ready.

activities.explanation: This stops when the clay has exactly the wetness needed for shaping.

activities.prompt: Appooppan has clay with different wetness. What is the fairest way to choose clay for shaping?
options: Try shaping; choose clay that is neither too watery nor dry.
Try shaping; choose the clay that is always the wettest.
Try shaping; choose the clay that is the driest.
Try shaping; choose clay that already has family patterns.

why.Try shaping; choose the clay that is alw: This chooses the wettest clay instead of clay that is just right.
why.Try shaping; choose the clay that is the: This chooses the driest clay instead of clay that is just right.
why.Try shaping; choose clay that already ha: This confuses a family pattern with how wet the clay is.

activities.title: Patterns All Around
activities.body: Mini helps her grandfather make and colour patterns on pots. Her favourite clay item is her piggy bank. She uses it to save money. Patterns appear in nature. Beautiful pottery comes from different parts of India.
keyPoints: Mini makes pot patterns and saves money.
Nature gives artists shapes, colours, and ideas.
Patterns may repeat shapes and lines.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects Mini's pot work with patterns found in nature.

activities.prompt: Mini wants to make a new pot pattern. Where can she look for ideas?
steps: Mini can look around nature, because patterns are found everywhere there.
She can use shapes and colours from nature, because artists get ideas there.
Animals can help too: a leopard has spots, and a squirrel has stripes.
So Mini can find ideas by noticing patterns in nature.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

Make new pots
Colour old pots
Choose clay items

activities.prompt: Mini uses her piggy bank to ______ money.

From empty clay shelves

Plain shapes without nature colours
Animal sounds instead of patterns

why.Plain shapes without nature colours: This wrongly leaves out nature's colours.
why.Animal sounds instead of patterns: This wrongly chooses sounds instead of visible patterns.

activities.explanation: Nature gives pot artists ideas for their art.

activities.body: Bricks are made of mud, like the pots made by Appooppan. The mud is placed in moulds to give bricks their shape. Then bricks are baked in a kiln, where they become hard. These hard bricks are used to make houses, schools and hospitals. Rohan lives in Jaipur with his father. Rohan enjoys watching houses and brick walls being built.

Baking bricks in a kiln makes them hard.
Bricks are used to build houses, schools and hospitals.

Hard bricks can build houses, schools and hospitals, so they are useful.

activities.title: Why people build mud houses
activities.body: Some warm areas have traditional mud houses. These houses help keep the inside cool. People use natural materials like grass and wood. Many people also use cow dung instead of cement. Cow dung can make smooth walls and smooth floors. It keeps heat out of the house and stops insects from entering.
keyPoints: Mud houses help keep the inside cool.
Grass and wood are natural materials.
Cow dung makes smooth surfaces and stops insects.
activities.explanation: Mud houses use helpful natural materials.

steps: People can use cow dung instead of cement because many do.
Cow dung can make smooth walls and smooth floors.
It keeps heat out of the house, so the inside stays cool.
It also stops insects from entering, making it a helpful material.

activities.prompt: What do mud houses help keep cool?

the inside
the grass
the wood

activities.prompt: Cow dung can make smooth walls. It also stops insects from entering. What happens when insects reach a cow-dung wall?

They stop before entering the house.

The child wrongly thinks insects make walls rough.
The child wrongly thinks insects cause extra heat.

activities.explanation: This is right because cow dung stops insects from entering.

Check whether people use grass as a natural material.

why.Check whether people use wood as a natur: The child checks wood, but the claim is about grass.
why.Check whether people use cow dung instea: The child checks cement use, not grass use.

activities.explanation: This is right because people do use grass as a natural material.

why.He also needs sturdy footwear, but not a: This forgets that a safety vest is also required.

why.Only atta dough can make bricks besides: This leaves out paper boxes, which can also make bricks.
why.Neither paper boxes nor atta dough can m: This wrongly treats clay as the only allowed brick material.

activities.prompt: Appooppan finds that the clay is too dry to shape properly. What should he do before spinning it on the stone wheel?

Move the clay into the kiln immediately

activities.context: Appooppan is Mini’s grandfather, and he makes pots. First, he makes the clay wet and adds water until it is just right for shaping. He pounds and kneads the clay well, like dough. Next, he shapes it by spinning it on a stone wheel. After the pots have dried, Ammu moves them into the very hot potter’s oven, which is called a kiln. activities.prompt: Why does Appooppan knead the clay like dough before shaping the pot?
options: To help the clay become ready for shaping

To dry the wet pot in the oven
To move the pot into the oven

why.To bake the clay inside the kiln: The clay must have the right wetness.
why.To dry the wet pot in the oven: The kiln is used for baking.

Because patterns on animals mean that the pot should have no shapes or lines.

why.Because the spots and stripes are the on: Incorrect: It mistakes natural patterns for a restricted colour list.
why.Because patterns on animals mean that th: Incorrect: It wrongly says natural patterns exclude shapes and lines.

activities.explanation: Correct: Nature gives artists ideas for their art.

activities.context: Mini watches her grandfather make and colour patterns on pots. Before painting, he looks at nature because artists get ideas for their art from nature. activities.prompt: Explain why patterns in nature can help Mini make a pot design.

activities.prompt: If the mud in a mould is never baked, what would happen to the brick?
options: It may remain unbaked mud and will not become a hard brick.
It will become hard because the mould gives it extra heat.
It will become hard as soon as the mud is placed in the mould.
It will become hard because the wall joins it to other bricks.

why.It will become hard because the mould gi: The mould gives the brick its shape; it does not provide the heat needed for baking.

activities.context: Rohan lives in Jaipur with his father. Because Rohan loves watching houses being built, he stays near the place where his father and his co-workers are building a wall. activities.prompt: What should Rohan watch to understand how a shaped brick becomes hard?

why.He should watch the bricks being made be: The brick is shaped when it is prepared in a mould, not before that step.
why.He should watch the wall being built wit: Avoiding the kiln would leave him without the step that makes bricks hard.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a brick before and after it is baked in a kiln.
activities.answer: Before baking, the brick has been given its shape in a mould. Baking it in a kiln makes the brick hard. The mould is important for shaping the brick, while the kiln is important for making it hard enough to use in buildings.

The kiln makes the brick hard.
Hard bricks can be used in buildings.

Remind him to put on sturdier footwear.

why.Remind him to leave the helmet strap loo: A loose strap does not follow the safety rule.
The safety vest should be worn at work.
Sturdier footwear does not secure the helmet strap.

activities.explanation: The strap is part of the helmet safety rule.

activities.context: Rohan’s father is making a wall at work. He wears a helmet with a strap, a safety vest, and sturdy footwear. In Rohan’s class activity, a matchbox mould is used to make bricks. The bricks may also be made from small paper boxes, clay, or atta dough. When they are ready, the bricks are stacked in two different arrangements.
activities.prompt: The class cannot use the matchbox mould for one activity. Which item can be used to make bricks?
options: paper boxes
the safety vest
the helmet
sturdy footwear

why.the safety vest: A safety vest is worn for protection.
why.the helmet: A helmet is worn on the head.
why.sturdy footwear: Sturdy footwear is worn on the feet.

activities.explanation: Small paper boxes can be used to make bricks.

activities.prompt: How does making bricks differ from stacking the bricks?
activities.answer: Making bricks means using a matchbox mould or using small paper boxes, clay, or atta dough. Stacking means placing the finished bricks in two different arrangements. One activity creates the bricks; the other places them after they are ready.
points: A matchbox mould can make bricks.
Small paper boxes, clay, and atta dough can also make bricks.
Stacking uses two different arrangements.
Stacking happens after the bricks are ready.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.title: Ready the clay
activities.prompt: Which step happens before Appooppan shapes the clay?
options: He adds water
He bakes the pot
He makes patterns
He builds a wall
activities.explanation: Appooppan adds water until the clay is just right for shaping.

activities.title: The right clay
activities.prompt: Appooppan makes the clay too watery before shaping it.
activities.explanation: The clay must be neither too watery nor too dry.

activities.title: The potter's oven
activities.prompt: The potter's oven is called a ______.
activities.hint: It is very hot.
activities.explanation: The fire in the kiln bakes the pot.

activities.title: Patterns around us
activities.prompt: Match each animal or plant with its pattern.
activities.explanation: Animals and plants around us can have patterns.

activities.title: Mini's favourite
activities.prompt: What does Mini use her piggy bank for?
options: Saving money
Making clay
Building walls
Baking pots
activities.explanation: Mini's favourite clay item is her piggy bank. She uses it to save money.

activities.title: Smooth homes
activities.prompt: Cow dung can make smooth floors.
activities.explanation: Cow dung can make smooth floors. It can also make smooth walls.

activities.title: Natural homes

activities.explanation: Mud houses stay cool, while cow dung keeps heat out. Grass and wood are natural materials.

activities.title: Hard bricks

activities.hint: A kiln is the potter's oven.
activities.explanation: Baking in the kiln makes a brick hard.

activities.title: Rohan's wall

items: Build the wall brick by brick
See the wall become a big building
activities.explanation: Rohan watched the wall grow brick by brick. After a few months, it became a big building.

activities.title: Safe at work
activities.prompt: Why does Rohan's father wear safety gear at work?
options: He follows safety rules
He saves his money
He makes clay patterns
He cools warm houses
activities.explanation: He wears a helmet, safety vest and sturdy footwear at work.

chapters.title: Taking Charge of Waste
chapters.summary: In this chapter: how waste is created and managed; reduce waste; reuse things; a place of pride.

lessons.title: How Waste Is Created and Managed

activities.prompt: Where does our rubbish go after we throw it away?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Waste around us
activities.body: Everyday activities create lots of waste. Old clothes, tins, bottles, paper and fruit and vegetable peels are thrown away. Some of this waste ends up in garbage piles near homes, schools and neighbourhoods. Wastewater is water that flows through roads. Animals can die after eating plastic mixed with food. We need to learn how to manage waste. We can learn from people and places that manage it well.
keyPoints: Everyday activities create waste.
Some waste ends up in garbage piles.
Plastic and wastewater can cause harm.
activities.explanation: This lesson explains where waste goes and why it matters.

activities.prompt: Garbage and plastic are near homes. How can we keep people and animals safe?
steps: Daily activities create waste, so we throw away clothes, bottles, and peels.
Garbage piles near homes need managing, because thrown-away waste gathers there.
Plastic mixed with food can kill animals, so it needs safe management.
Garbage can make people ill, so learn from places managing waste well.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement is true about waste?
options: Everyday activities create waste.
Garbage piles are far from homes.
We do not need to manage waste.
Animals are safe from plastic.
activities.explanation: Everyday activities create a lot of waste. This is true.

activities.prompt: What is often found on roadsides near houses and yards?
options: Trash
Food
Water
Clean air
activities.explanation: Trash is often found on roadsides near houses and yards. This is true.

activities.prompt: Some thrown-away waste ends up in ______ piles.
activities.hint: These piles can be seen around homes, schools and neighbourhoods.
activities.explanation: Some thrown-away waste ends up in garbage piles. These piles can be seen around homes and schools.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what can happen or where it goes.
activities.explanation: Animals can die after eating plastic mixed with food. Wastewater can carry germs that cause other diseases.

activities.prompt: Put these stages in order.
items: Old clothes, tins, bottles, paper and fruit and vegetable peels are thrown away
Some thrown-away waste ends up in garbage piles
activities.explanation: First, activities create waste. Then, some waste is thrown away and ends up in garbage piles.

activities.prompt: What can wastewater carry?
options: Harmful gases
Germs
Mosquitoes
Old clothes
activities.explanation: Wastewater can carry germs that cause other diseases. This matches the lesson.

activities.prompt: A family throws away bottles and fruit peels near a house. Where will much of the waste go?
options: Inside clean school books
In fresh drinking cups
In garbage piles near homes
Under soft sleeping beds

why.Inside clean school books: This mistakes waste for paper that is still being used.
why.In fresh drinking cups: This mistakes waste for containers that are still being used.
why.Under soft sleeping beds: This assumes waste is placed under beds.

activities.explanation: Thrown-away bottles and peels often end up in garbage piles near homes.

activities.prompt: Wastewater flows through a road near houses. What may happen next?
options: Fewer mosquitoes may appear nearby
The road may dry up faster
More mosquitoes may appear nearby
The germs may disappear at once

why.Fewer mosquitoes may appear nearby: This assumes wastewater makes fewer mosquitoes, not more.
why.The road may dry up faster: This thinks wastewater only changes how roads dry.
why.The germs may disappear at once: This assumes wastewater removes germs and mosquitoes at once.

activities.explanation: Wastewater flowing through roads can lead to more mosquitoes.

activities.prompt: Wastewater carries germs through a road. What may happen to people?
options: Some people may get other diseases
Every person will stay healthy
The water will cure all diseases
No germ will spread through it

why.Every person will stay healthy: This assumes all people stay healthy around wastewater.
why.The water will cure all diseases: This assumes wastewater cures diseases instead of carrying germs.
why.No germ will spread through it: This assumes germs cannot spread through wastewater.

activities.explanation: Wastewater can carry germs that cause other diseases.

lessons.sceneCaption: Indore’s clean streets show the results of planned and organised waste management.

lessons.title: Reduce Waste

activities.prompt: What simple ways can we help our planet every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways to Reduce Waste
activities.body: The first rule is to reduce the amount of waste we create. Many people avoid buying food and drinks packed in wrappers or plastic bottles. Using cloth bags instead of plastic bags helps to reduce waste. The Cleanliness Drive also includes sharing. We can share our old toys and books with people who need them. Buy only what you need. Use things until they cannot be used anymore.
keyPoints: Reduce the waste we create.
Use cloth bags and avoid packed wrappers or plastic bottles.
Share old things, buy only what we need, and use things fully.
activities.explanation: Small choices like sharing, buying only what you need, and using things fully can reduce waste.

activities.prompt: Your old toy is no longer needed. What should you do with it?
steps: Keep only what you need, because buying more can create waste.
Share it with someone who needs it, so it gets another use.
Keep using it until it cannot be used, to make less waste.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do many people avoid buying?
options: Food and drinks in wrappers or bottles
Old toys and books for others
Cloth bags for shopping
Things that people need
activities.explanation: Many people avoid buying food and drinks in wrappers or plastic bottles.

activities.prompt: We can share our old ______ and books with people who need them.
activities.hint: The Cleanliness Drive includes sharing things with others.
activities.explanation: Old toys and books can be shared with people who need them. Sharing things is part of the Cleanliness Drive.

activities.prompt: What happens when people buy more things?
options: They use old toys longer.
They share more books.
They throw away more things.
They need fewer things.
activities.explanation: Buying more things makes us throw away more things. This is why we should buy only what we need.

activities.prompt: Match each action to what happens when we do it.
pairs: Use things until they cannot be used
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an action with its result. Together, these actions help us reduce waste.

activities.prompt: Which action follows the first rule for reducing waste?
options: Buying more things
Buying only what you need
Packing food in wrappers
Avoiding sharing things
activities.explanation: The first rule is to reduce the amount of waste we create. Buying only what we need follows this rule.

activities.prompt: Which set follows the lesson's waste-saving rules?
options: Buy more; share old books; use things fully.
Buy what you need; throw away toys; use things fully.
Buy only what you need; share old books; use things fully.
Buy only what you need; share old books; stop using useful things.
activities.explanation: This choice buys only what is needed, shares old books, and uses things fully. All three actions help reduce waste.

activities.prompt: A child buys many extra things. What is likely to happen over time?
options: More things will be thrown away.
Fewer things will be thrown away.
Things will be used for longer.
Less waste will be created.

This wrongly assumes buying more reduces what is thrown away.
This wrongly assumes extra things are used for longer.
This wrongly assumes extra buying creates less waste.

activities.explanation: Buying more things makes us throw away more things.

activities.prompt: You want a new toy, but you do not need it. What is the best choice?
options: Buy it because you want a new toy.
Buy it because your friends have one.
Do not buy it because you do not need it.
Buy it and share it after one use.

Buying only what we need helps reduce waste.
This confuses wanting something with needing it.
Sharing is good, but buying an unneeded toy still adds waste.

activities.explanation: This assumes a friend's choice shows what we need.

activities.prompt: One child has a cloth bag. Another has a plastic bag. Which test is fairest?
options: Use each bag for the same shopping, then compare waste.
Use the cloth bag for extra shopping, then compare waste.
Use the plastic bag for extra shopping, then compare waste.
Throw both bags away, then compare their waste.

why.Use the cloth bag for extra shopping, th: Extra shopping changes both the bag type and the shopping amount.
why.Use the plastic bag for extra shopping,: Extra shopping also changes both the bag type and the shopping amount.
why.Throw both bags away, then compare their: Throwing both bags away does not test using them instead.

activities.explanation: Same shopping keeps the bag type as the main change.

lessons.sceneAlt: A shop at the ISKCON Campus in Mayapur displays several fabric bags that can be used instead of plastic bags.
lessons.sceneCaption: Reusable fabric bags at a Mayapur shop help reduce plastic waste.

lessons.title: Reuse Things

activities.prompt: What clever ways can we give old things a new life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Many Uses for Old Things
activities.body: Our grandparents did not throw away old clothes. They made quilts from old sarees and bags from old clothes. They gave old clothes to people who needed clothes. Old newspapers and cloth can become gift wrapping. This way is eco-friendly and reduces waste. We can reuse one-sided paper for rough work. We can refill steel or copper bottles. We can make toys and decorations from old newspapers and calendars.
keyPoints: Old clothes can become useful items.
Reused wrapping reduces waste.
Paper and bottles can be used again.
activities.explanation: Reusing things helps us waste less and find new uses for them.

activities.prompt: A gift needs wrapping. What can we use, and why?
steps: Old newspaper and cloth can wrap the gift because both can be used for wrapping.
This choice is eco-friendly because reusing them reduces waste.
Therefore, use old newspaper or cloth for the wrapper.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which action did our grandparents take with old clothes?
options: Made toys from old clothes.
Made bags from old clothes.
Made decorations from old clothes.
Threw old clothes away.
activities.explanation: Good choice! Our grandparents made bags from old clothes.

activities.prompt: Grandparents made a ______ from old sarees.
activities.hint: They made it from old sarees.
activities.explanation: Great! Our grandparents made quilts from old sarees.

activities.prompt: Match each item to its reuse.
activities.explanation: Old sarees make quilts, and old clothes make bags. Old newspapers and cloth are reused for gift wrapping.

activities.prompt: Which environmental benefit does eco-friendly gift wrapping give?
options: It creates more waste.
It needs extra plastic.
It reduces waste.
It needs more electricity.
activities.explanation: Reusing old newspapers and cloth reduces waste. This gift-wrapping method is eco-friendly.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for reusing a gift in order.
items: Give it to someone who helps keep the locality or home clean.
activities.explanation: Wrapping comes before giving the gift. The recipient can help keep the locality or home clean.

activities.prompt: Which plan reuses two things and follows the lesson?
options: Make a paper bag with glue and refill a steel bottle.
Refill a steel bottle and reuse old cloth.
Throw away old clothes and reuse one-sided paper.
Use new wrapping and refill a steel bottle.
activities.explanation: A steel bottle can be refilled and reused. Old cloth can also be used for gift wrapping.

activities.prompt: Old newspaper and cloth can wrap a gift. What happens if we reuse them?
options: The gift is wrapped, and less waste is made.
The gift stays unwrapped, and more waste is made.
Only the paper is used, so the cloth is wasted.
Both materials are used, but the gift is not wrapped.

why.The gift stays unwrapped, and more waste: This wrongly assumes old materials cannot wrap a gift.
why.Only the paper is used, so the cloth is: This wrongly thinks cloth cannot be used for wrapping.
why.Both materials are used, but the gift is: This wrongly thinks using them means the gift stays unwrapped.

activities.explanation: Reused wrapping uses these materials and reduces waste.

activities.prompt: A paper sheet has writing on one side. The other side is clean. How can we use it well?
options: Write on one side, then use the other side for rough work.
Use both sides, then throw the paper away now.
Use the clean side, then give the written side away.
Use the written side, then make the blank side dirty.

why.Use both sides, then throw the paper awa: This throws away a side that could still be used.
why.Use the clean side, then give the writte: This gives away the written side instead of reusing it.
why.Use the written side, then make the blan: This wastes the blank side instead of using it for rough work.

activities.explanation: This uses the paper twice for different kinds of work.

activities.prompt: Your grandparents have old clothes. Some people need clothes, and a quilt is wanted. What should they do?
options: Give some clothes away and make a quilt.
Give all clothes away and make no quilt.
Make only bags and give no clothes away.
Make a bag and give all clothes away.

This wrongly leaves the wanted quilt undone.
This wrongly thinks bags are the only useful reuse for clothes.
This wrongly makes a bag instead of the wanted quilt.

activities.explanation: This gives needed clothes away and also makes a quilt.

lessons.sceneCaption: Reusable wrapping paper and newspapers appear inside a Japanese library.

lessons.title: A Place of Pride

activities.prompt: How do some villages and cities keep their surroundings so clean and beautiful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Silluk: A Zero Waste Village
activities.body: Many villages and cities once had garbage all around them. Some may now be the cleanest areas in the country. Silluk is a village in Arunachal Pradesh. Its roads are clean, with no trash on roadsides, in corners, or in open spaces. This is why it is called a zero waste village. Tree-lined streets feel like a garden. Silluk received an award for managing its waste well.
keyPoints: Many places once had garbage around them.
Silluk has clean roads and no trash outside.
Silluk is called a zero waste village.
activities.explanation: Good waste management helps keep Silluk clean.

activities.prompt: Many villages and cities once had garbage around them. How can we check whether Silluk is now clean and proud?
steps: We look outside because many places once had garbage around them.
Silluk has no trash on roadsides, corners, or open spaces.
Its clean, tree-lined streets also feel like a garden.
Its award and zero waste village name show pride in cleanliness.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which place is Silluk?
options: A village in Arunachal Pradesh
A city in Arunachal Pradesh
An Arunachal Pradesh city
An Arunachal Pradesh town
activities.explanation: Silluk is a village in Arunachal Pradesh. You found the right place!

activities.prompt: Match each place with its description.
pairs: stands out as a clean city
activities.explanation: Each place matches the description given in the lesson. Well done!

activities.prompt: Which name is given to Silluk?
options: Zero waste village
Waste-free city
Garden streets village
Waste award city
activities.explanation: Silluk is called a zero waste village. Its streets have no trash.

activities.prompt: Silluk received an ______ for managing its waste well.
activities.hint: This is something a village can receive.
activities.explanation: An award was given to Silluk for managing its waste well.

activities.prompt: Which village was among the first to become waste-free?
options: Chhota Narena village
Silluk village
Mysuru city
Indore city
activities.explanation: Chhota Narena was among the first villages to become waste-free.

activities.prompt: Why do Silluk's tree-lined streets feel like a garden?
options: Because its streets are lined with trees.
Because its roadsides hold lots of trash.
Because its corners are full of waste.
Because its open spaces have rubbish.
activities.explanation: Tree-lined streets make Silluk feel like a garden. That is the reason.

activities.prompt: Silluk has clean roads and no roadside trash. A visitor drops rubbish. What should happen next?
options: The visitor picks it up and keeps the road clean.
The visitor leaves it because other roads have trash.
The rubbish stays there because awards allow any mess.
The visitor moves it to a corner and hides the mess.

why.The visitor leaves it because other road: This wrongly assumes other roads still have rubbish.
why.The rubbish stays there because awards a: This wrongly thinks an award allows rubbish to stay outside.
why.The visitor moves it to a corner and hid: This wrongly treats a corner as a proper place for rubbish.

activities.explanation: This is right because litter would spoil Silluk's clean roads.

activities.prompt: You want to check if a village manages its waste well now. What is the fairest test?
options: Look for trash on roadsides, corners, and open spaces.
Trust only an award, without checking the village.
Check whether many trees line the village streets.
Count the cleanest roads in the whole country.

why.Trust only an award, without checking th: This wrongly trusts an award without checking current conditions.
why.Check whether many trees line the villag: This wrongly treats tree-lined streets as proof of waste management.
why.Count the cleanest roads in the whole co: This wrongly checks the whole country instead of one village.

activities.explanation: This is right because it checks where rubbish is left.

activities.prompt: Silluk is a zero waste village and has a waste award. A child says the award proves the name. Why is this weak?
options: An award shows good waste management, not zero waste itself.
An award proves that every place has no rubbish.
Tree-lined streets prove a village is zero waste.
Waste-free villages cannot receive waste awards.

why.An award proves that every place has no: This wrongly treats one village's award as proof about every place.
why.Tree-lined streets prove a village is ze: This wrongly treats clean-looking streets as proof of zero waste.
why.Waste-free villages cannot receive waste: This wrongly denies what is known about Silluk.

activities.explanation: This is right because an award does not create the zero waste name.

activities.prompt: Chhota Narena was among the first villages to become waste-free. What can we learn from this?
options: Waste-free villages can exist and show other villages a way.
Chhota Narena must be the only waste-free village.
A village must win an award before becoming waste-free.
Only the earliest village can manage waste well.

why.Chhota Narena must be the only waste-fre: This wrongly turns among the first into only one.
why.A village must win an award before becom: This wrongly assumes that an award must come before waste-free work.
why.Only the earliest village can manage was: This wrongly believes only the first village can succeed.

activities.explanation: This is right because Chhota Narena shows that waste-free villages are possible.

activities.prompt: Indore and Mysuru are known as clean cities. A sign links one city's cleanliness to the other. Why is that weak?
options: One clean city cannot prove another clean city is clean.
Both cities must be villages before they can be clean.
One city's trees can make another city clean.
One city's award can prove every other city is clean.

why.Both cities must be villages before they: This wrongly treats clean cities as zero waste villages.
why.One city's trees can make another city c: This wrongly transfers tree-lined streets between different places.
why.One city's award can prove every other c: This wrongly treats Silluk's award as proof about every city.

activities.explanation: This is right because each city is known as clean on its own.

lessons.sceneAlt: A tree-lined road passes through Mawlynnong Village, a settlement in Meghalaya noted for its cleanliness.
lessons.sceneCaption: Mawlynnong Village in Meghalaya is noted for its cleanliness, with tree-lined roads and village buildings.

lessons.title: Separate Different Types of Waste

activities.prompt: Which dustbin should each kind of waste go into?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Green and Blue Dustbins
activities.body: Green and blue dustbins help us separate waste. The green dustbin takes dry leaves, branches, fruit peels, vegetable waste and eggshells. This waste rots easily and mixes with soil to become compost. Compost feeds plants and tiny soil animals. The blue dustbin takes metal, glass and plastic. New objects can be made from these discarded materials and paper. This is called recycling.
keyPoints: Green dustbins take garden and kitchen waste.
Blue dustbins take metal, glass and plastic.
Recycling makes new objects from discarded materials.
activities.explanation: Different dustbins help us handle different kinds of waste.

activities.prompt: A child has leaves, fruit peels, and a metal can. Which bins should they use?
steps: Dry leaves and fruit peels fit the green dustbin's list.
This waste rots easily and mixes with soil, becoming compost.
Compost gives food to plants and tiny soil animals.
The metal can belongs in blue, because blue takes metal.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What belongs in the green dustbin?
options: Dry leaves and branches
Metal and glass
Metal and plastic
Glass and plastic
activities.explanation: The green dustbin takes dry leaves and branches. It also takes fruit peels, vegetable waste and eggshells.

activities.prompt: The blue dustbin takes dry leaves and branches.
activities.explanation: The green dustbin takes dry leaves and branches. The blue dustbin takes metal, glass and plastic.

activities.prompt: The ______ dustbin takes metal, glass and plastic.
activities.hint: Choose the bin that does not take dry leaves.
activities.explanation: The blue dustbin takes things made of metal, glass and plastic.

activities.prompt: Match each material with its bin or benefit.
activities.explanation: Green-bin waste becomes compost. Compost provides food for plants and tiny soil animals.

activities.prompt: Put these compost-making steps in order.
items: Green-bin waste is added to soil
activities.explanation: Green-bin waste added to soil becomes compost. This compost then provides food for plants.

activities.prompt: What is making new objects from discarded materials called?
options: Recycling
Compost
Separate
Rot
activities.explanation: Making new objects from discarded metal, glass, plastic and paper is called recycling.

activities.prompt: Compost provides food for plants and tiny soil animals.
activities.explanation: Compost provides food for plants and tiny soil animals. It forms from green-bin waste added to soil.

activities.prompt: Which action best follows the lesson?
options: Separate waste and recycle materials.
Mix leaves, glass and metal together.
Keep vegetable waste with plastic.
Use the same bin for everything.
activities.explanation: Separating waste and recycling materials helps villages and towns keep their surroundings clean.

activities.prompt: Leaves and branches go into the green dustbin. What happens next?
options: They mix with soil and can become compost.
They stay dry and never mix with soil.
They turn into metal and glass objects.
They must all go into the blue dustbin.

This mistake thinks green-bin waste will not rot or mix.
This mistake treats leaves like materials for metal or glass.
This mistake sends green-bin waste to the wrong dustbin.

activities.explanation: This is right because green-bin waste rots and mixes with soil.

activities.prompt: Compost can feed plants and tiny soil animals. Which test is fair?
options: Compare soil with compost and soil without compost.
Put compost in the blue dustbin and wait.
Compare two green dustbins in different places.
Add metal and glass to soil and watch.

why.Put compost in the blue dustbin and wait: This mistake puts compost in a bin instead of testing soil.
why.Compare two green dustbins in different: This mistake compares bin places instead of soil and compost.
This mistake tests metal and glass instead of compost.

activities.explanation: This is fair because it compares soil with and without compost.
